title: Overview
content:
Here's the practical core — the stuff that shows up in nearly every conversation, versus the long tail of patterns that are mostly for reading/writing or exam nuance.

## 1. Particles are the skeleton
Japanese word order is flexible because particles mark grammatical role, not position. Six carry almost all daily conversation:
- **は** — topic ("as for X...")
- **が** — subject/emphasis (subtly different from は — the classic hard-to-explain pair, but daily use is learnable by pattern before theory)
- **を** — direct object
- **に / で** — に for time/destination/indirect object, で for location-of-action/means
- **の** — possession/linking nouns
- **と / も** — "and/with" for people, "also"

## 2. The て-form is the hub of the language
This is the single highest-leverage thing to master. Once you can form it, it unlocks most of daily grammar by just attaching things to it:
- 食べて + ください → please eat
- 食べて + いる → eating (progressive/state)
- 食べて + もいい → allowed to eat
- 食べて + はいけない → not allowed to eat
- 食べて + みる → try eating
- 食べて + おく → eat in preparation
- 食べて、飲んで、寝た → sequencing actions

If you only drill one conjugation hard, make it this one.

## 3. Register: plain form vs です/ます
Daily life constantly switches between polite (strangers, coworkers, service) and plain/casual (friends, family, inner thoughts). You need both forms of everything — this isn't optional politeness, it's a structural axis of the grammar (plain form is also what's used inside longer sentences, e.g. before と思う).

## 4. A small set of workhorse patterns
These cover a disproportionate share of real speech:
- **〜たい** — want to do
- **〜たら** — if/when (the most flexible, casual conditional — skip ば/と/なら until たら feels natural)
- **〜と思う** — I think
- **〜んです** — explanatory nuance ("the thing is...") — extremely common in natural speech, rarely taught early
- **あげる/くれる/もらう** — giving and receiving, direction-of-favor matters a lot socially in Japanese
- **〜ことができる / 動詞可能形** — ability

## 5. Sentence-final particles
ね (seeking agreement), よ (asserting new info), か (question), わ (softening) — these get skipped in formal grammar study but carry enormous conversational nuance. Native daily speech barely exists without them.

---

Everything else — causative-passive, formal written forms, most of the "hundred patterns" — is long-tail: useful eventually, low-frequency in daily talk. If you want, this list could double as the actual skeleton for your notes draft, grouped as "core" vs "everything else," rather than following the guide's chronological lesson order.

title: は - topic particle
content:
# は - topic particle

Marks what the sentence is *about* — sets the frame, then says something about it. Read as "wa" (not "ha") when used as a particle.

## Core pattern
**X は Y** → "as for X, Y" / "speaking of X, it's Y"

- 私は学生です。— I'm a student. (as for me, [I'm a] student)
- これは本です。— This is a book.
- 東京は大きいです。— Tokyo is big.

## What it actually does
は doesn't mark the grammatical subject — it marks the **topic**. The topic can be the subject, but doesn't have to be:

- 象は鼻が長い。— Elephants, [their] trunk is long. (topic: elephant, subject of 長い: 鼻)
- この店はラーメンがおいしい。— This shop, the ramen is good. (topic: shop, subject: ramen)

This is why は and が can coexist in the same sentence — they're not competing for the same job.

## は vs が (the classic pain point)
Don't try to fully resolve this early — pattern-match instead:

| Use は | Use が |
|---|---|
| Introducing what you're talking about | Introducing new information |
| Known/already-established topic | Answering "who/what" questions |
| General statements, contrast | Specific, in-the-moment observation |
| 私は田中です。(self-intro) | 誉が来た。(が for "who came") |

Quick test: if the question is "what about X?" → は. If the question is "what/who is it?" → が.

- 田中さんは先生です。— Mr. Tanaka is a teacher. (talking about Tanaka)
- だれが先生ですか。— Who is the teacher? / 田中さんが先生です。— Tanaka is [the one who's] the teacher. (が picks him out of a group)

## Contrast use
は can single something out in contrast to something else (often left unsaid):

- 魚は食べますが、肉は食べません。— I eat fish, but I don't eat meat.
- 日本語は話せますが、中国語は話せません。— I can speak Japanese, but not Chinese.

This contrastive は can attach to almost any part of a sentence, not just the subject:

- 今日は行きません。— [Unlike other days,] today I'm not going.

## Negation magnet
Negative sentences pull を/が toward は even when the noun isn't the "topic" in a strong sense — this is extremely common:

- パンを食べません。→ パンは食べません。— I don't eat bread.

## Notes
- は replaces を and が entirely (never は and を/が together on the same noun).
- With に/で/と/から etc., は stacks after the particle: 東京には行きました。(added emphasis/contrast — "to Tokyo, [at least,] I went")
- Topic doesn't have to be repeated once established — Japanese drops it constantly once context is clear.

title: が - subject/emphasis particle
content:
# が - subject/emphasis particle

Marks the grammatical subject, with a flavor of "this one specifically" — pointing at *who/what* does or is something, often as new or highlighted information. See [[1a-は]] for the full は-vs-が comparison table.

## Core pattern
**X が Y** → "X is the one that Y" / introduces X as the answer

- 猫がいます。— There's a cat. (announcing its existence)
- 誰が来ましたか。— Who came? / 田中さんが来ました。— Tanaka came.
- 雨が降っています。— It's raining. (rain as the subject of the observed event)

## New information / answering "who/what"
が is the natural choice when you're identifying something out of a group, or stating a fact for the first time:

- あの人が犯人です。— That person is the culprit. (picking them out)
- どれがあなたのですか。— Which one is yours? / これが私のです。— This one is mine.

Contrast with は, which would sound like "that person, [as for them,] is the culprit" — fine, but less natural as a first-mention answer.

## Objects of feeling/ability/desire
A large chunk of が's daily use isn't about "subject" at all — certain predicates just grammatically require が for their object:

- 日本語が分かります。— I understand Japanese.
- コーヒーが好きです。— I like coffee.
- 車がほしいです。— I want a car.
- 漢字が読めます。— I can read kanji. (potential form)

These aren't は/が contrast cases — the thing liked/wanted/understood/able-to-be-done is marked with が, full stop, even though English treats it like an object ("I like coffee" → coffee = object, but Japanese treats it as what's inducing the feeling in you).

## Subordinate clauses: が where は can't go
Inside a relative clause or subordinate clause modifying a noun, the subject is marked with が (not は), even if it would take は as a main-clause topic:

- 私が作った料理です。— This is the food [that] I made.
- 猫がいる家。— A house where there's a cat.

This is the same mechanic behind 象は鼻が長い (see [[1a-は]]) — が marks the local subject inside the descriptive part, while は sets the overall topic.

## Emphatic contrast (the opposite direction of は)
が can also emphasize "X and only X," gently excluding alternatives — often felt as slightly assertive or corrective:

- 僕がやります。— I'll do it. (I'm the one who will — not someone else)
- それが問題です。— That's the problem. (that one specifically)

## Notes
- が cannot stack with を or は on the same noun — it replaces them.
- Beginners overuse は and underuse が — if you're introducing something for the first time or answering a "who/what" question, reach for が.

title: を - direct object particle
content:
# を - direct object particle

Marks the thing a verb acts on. Read as "o" (the を kana is basically only used for this particle).

## Core pattern
**X を Verb** → "[do Verb] to/on X"

- パンを食べます。— I eat bread.
- 本を読みます。— I read a book.
- テレビを見ます。— I watch TV.

## Movement through/away from a space
A distinct use: を marks the space a motion verb passes through or departs from, not something being "acted on":

- 公園を歩きます。— I walk through the park.
- 道を渡ります。— I cross the street.
- 家を出ます。— I leave the house.
- 空を飛ぶ鳥。— A bird that flies through the sky.

Don't confuse this with に/で for destinations/locations — を is specifically the path or point of departure, not a fixed location.

## Dropped constantly in speech
In casual conversation, を is one of the first things to disappear. If the object is clear from context, native speakers routinely skip it — especially with common verbs:

- ご飯食べた? — (Did you) eat? (skipping ご飯を)
- 水ちょうだい。— Give me water. (skipping 水を)
- 何する? — What are you gonna do? (skipping 何を)

This is different from omitting the object entirely (which also happens once it's established in context) — here the noun stays, only the particle drops. It sounds natural and casual, not sloppy; but keep を in polite/written Japanese, and when the sentence would otherwise be ambiguous.

## Notes
- を cannot stack with は/が on the same noun — は or が replaces it under topic/contrast or negation (see [[1a-は]] "negation magnet").
- Some set expressions use を with verbs that don't feel like classic "objects": 旅行をする (to travel), 質問をする (to ask a question) — grammatically the noun+する combo takes を on the noun part.

title: に - time / destination / indirect object particle
content:
# に - time / destination / indirect object particle

に marks a fixed point: a point in time, a point you move toward, a point something exists at, or the person/thing on the receiving end of an action. See [[3b-で]] for the に-vs-で comparison.

## Time
Specific points in time (clock times, dates, days of week) take に. Relative time words (今日, 明日, 毎日, etc.) usually don't:

- 7時に起きます。— I get up at 7.
- 月曜日に行きます。— I'll go on Monday.
- 2020年に生まれました。— [I] was born in 2020.
- ~~今日に行きます~~ → 今日行きます。— I'll go today. (no に)

## Destination (motion toward a point)
With 行く/来る/帰る and similar verbs, に marks where you're headed:

- 学校に行きます。— I'm going to school.
- 家に帰ります。— I'm going home.
- 東京に来ました。— [I] came to Tokyo.

へ can substitute for this use (softer, more "in the direction of"), but に is the default and also does more jobs へ can't.

## Existence / location of being
With いる/ある (existence verbs), に marks where something is located — not で:

- 猫が部屋にいます。— The cat is in the room.
- 机の上に本があります。— There's a book on the desk.

## Indirect object (the receiver)
に marks the person something is given to, said to, sent to, taught to — the "to X" of "give X to Y":

- 友達にプレゼントをあげました。— I gave a present to my friend.
- 先生に聞きました。— I asked the teacher.
- メールを田中さんに送りました。— I sent an email to Tanaka.

## Purpose (before a movement verb)
Verb stem + に + movement verb = "go/come [in order] to do":

- 昼ご飯を食べに行きます。— I'm going to eat lunch.
- 映画を見に行きました。— [I] went to see a movie.

## に vs で — the key split
Both can look like "at/in [place]," but they're not interchangeable:

| に | で |
|---|---|
| Where something **exists** (いる/ある) | Where an **action happens** |
| Fixed point in time | — |
| Destination of motion | Means/instrument of doing something |
| 部屋にいます。(I'm in the room — existing) | 部屋で勉強します。(I study in the room — acting) |

Rule of thumb: if the verb is いる/ある or a "arrive-at" verb, use に. If the verb describes an activity happening in a place, use で. See [[3b-で]] for the full breakdown from で's side.

## Notes
- に can stack after は/も for topic/contrast: 東京には行きました。(see [[1a-は]])
- に also marks the agent in passive/causative sentences (先生に叱られた — was scolded by the teacher) — long-tail, not needed early.

title: で - location-of-action / means particle
content:
# で - location-of-action / means particle

で marks the setting an action takes place in, or the tool/method used to do it. See [[3a-に]] for the に-vs-で comparison.

## Location of action
When a verb describes something happening (not just existing), で marks where it happens:

- 公園で遊びます。— [I] play in the park.
- レストランで食べました。— [I] ate at a restaurant.
- 図書館で勉強します。— [I] study at the library.

Compare with いる/ある, which take に instead — see the split below.

## Means / instrument
で marks the tool, method, or medium used to do something — "by means of," "with," "using":

- 電車で行きます。— [I] go by train.
- はしで食べます。— [I] eat with chopsticks.
- 日本語で話しました。— [I] spoke in Japanese.
- ペンで書いてください。— Please write with a pen.

## Cause/reason
で can mark the cause behind a state or event, especially with natural causes or circumstances:

- 風邪で休みました。— [I] took the day off because of a cold.
- 事故で電車が止まった。— The train stopped due to an accident.

## Scope/limit ("within X")
で can mark a bounding quantity, time limit, or group:

- 3人で行きます。— [We] go as a group of 3.
- 1時間でできます。— [It] can be done within an hour.
- 全部で1000円です。— It's 1000 yen in total.

## に vs で — the key split
The classic beginner trap is choosing between に and で for "at/in [place]." They split along **existence vs. action**:

| で | に |
|---|---|
| Where an **action happens** | Where something **exists** (いる/ある) |
| Means/instrument of doing something | Fixed point in time |
| — | Destination of motion |
| 部屋で勉強します。(studying — an action happening in the room) | 部屋にいます。(existing — just being in the room) |

A useful test: can you meaningfully ask "doing what, there?" — if yes, で. If the sentence is really just answering "where is it," そこにある/いる territory — に.

Some verbs genuinely take either depending on what you mean: 公園に集まる (gather at — arriving at a point) vs 公園で集まって遊ぶ (gather and play — action happening there). See [[3a-に]] for the full breakdown from に's side.

## Notes
- で also marks the material something is made from: 木で作った椅子。— A chair made of wood.
- で can stack after topic/contrast は: 電車では行きません。— [I] won't go by train (implying some other way).

title: の - possession / noun-linking particle
content:
# の - possession / noun-linking particle

Links two nouns together, most commonly as possession, but really it's a general "noun's noun" connector.

## Possession
**X の Y** → "X's Y" / "Y of X"

- 私の本。— My book.
- 田中さんの車。— Tanaka's car.
- 日本の首都。— The capital of Japan.

## Noun modifying noun (broader than possession)
の links any noun to another noun, describing/categorizing it — often where English uses a compound noun or "of":

- 英語の先生。— English teacher. (teacher of English)
- 大学の友達。— A friend from university.
- 木の机。— A wooden desk. (desk of wood)
- 日本語の本。— A Japanese[-language] book.

## Nominalizer (turning a clause into a noun)
の can turn a whole verb/adjective clause into something you can talk about as a thing — very common in casual explanation and with こと-like structures:

- 走るのが好きです。— [I] like running. (running, [that thing], is liked)
- 漢字を読むのは難しい。— Reading kanji is hard.
- 財布を忘れたのに気づいた。— [I] noticed that [I'd] forgotten my wallet.

This is functionally close to こと, but の is preferred for things you can perceive directly (見る/聞く/気づく) or habitual/immediate actions, while こと fits more abstract statements — a fine distinction to not over-worry about early.

## Explanatory の (spoken, casual んです's cousin)
At the end of a sentence, の (often contracted to ん, as in 〜んです) adds an explanatory/seeking-clarification tone:

- どうしたの? — What's wrong? (seeking an explanation)
- 遅れたの。— [I'm explaining:] I was late.

This overlaps heavily with 〜んです — see the workhorse patterns note in [[0-overview]].

## Chaining
の can chain multiple times:

- 私の母の車。— My mother's car.
- 日本の会社の社長。— The president of a Japanese company.

## Pronoun-like の (omitting a repeated noun)
の can stand in for a noun already established, avoiding repetition:

- 私の本と彼の(本)。— My book and his (one).
- 赤いのをください。— Please give me the red one.

## Notes
- Unlike English "of," の always goes X の Y with X first — order never flips.
- の doesn't stack with は/が/を on the noun it attaches to a preceding noun; it just links nouns directly.

title: と - "and/with" (people, exhaustive lists) particle
content:
# と - "and/with" (people, exhaustive lists) particle

Links nouns exhaustively ("and"), or marks a companion/counterpart for an action done together. See [[5b-も]] for how と differs from も's "also" role.

## Exhaustive "and" (complete list)
と lists all the items — nothing left out. Contrast with や (not covered in the core set), which implies "and others":

- パンとコーヒーを買いました。— I bought bread and coffee. (only those two things)
- 犬と猫がいます。— There's a dog and a cat.

## "With" (companion)
と marks who you do something together with — the co-participant, not the object:

- 友達と映画を見ました。— I watched a movie with a friend.
- 一人で行くより、家族と行きたい。— Rather than going alone, I want to go with family.

Compare: 友達に会いました (I met [ran into] a friend, に marks the target) vs 友達と会いました (I met up with a friend, と marks doing it together, more planned/mutual).

## Quoting / reporting speech and thought
と marks the content of what's said, thought, called, or written — pairs constantly with 言う/思う/聞く:

- 「行きます」と言いました。— [He] said, "I'll go."
- 明日雨が降ると思います。— I think it'll rain tomorrow.
- これは日本語で「猫」と言います。— This is called "neko" in Japanese.

This is the と behind the workhorse pattern 〜と思う (see [[0-overview]]) — always plain form before と思う, even in polite sentences.

## Conditional "if/when" (と-conditional)
と can form a conditional meaning "whenever X happens, Y naturally follows" — mechanical/automatic relationships, not one-off choices:

- 春になると、花が咲きます。— When spring comes, flowers bloom.
- このボタンを押すと、電気がつきます。— If you press this button, the light turns on.

Less flexible than たら for everyday hypothetical situations — see the note on たら in [[0-overview]] for why that's usually the better default.

## Reciprocal verbs
Certain verbs describing mutual action pair naturally with と since the action inherently involves two sides:

- 彼と結婚しました。— [I] married him.
- 隣の人と喧嘩した。— [I] had a fight with my neighbor.

## Notes
- と can't be dropped the way を is — it's load-bearing for clarity in "and" lists and quoting.
- と can stack with は for contrast: 彼とは話しません。— I won't talk with him [implying: unlike others].

title: も - "also/too" particle
content:
# も - "also/too" particle

Marks something as being included alongside something else — "also," "too," or (in negative sentences) "not... either." See [[5a-と]] for how も differs from と's exhaustive-list role.

## Basic "also/too"
も replaces は/が/を on the noun it attaches to — it doesn't stack with them:

- 私も学生です。— I'm also a student. (implying someone else already was mentioned)
- コーヒーも飲みます。— [I] drink coffee too.
- 田中さんも来ました。— Tanaka came too.

Compare with と: 私と田中さん (me and Tanaka, listed together in one clause) vs 私も行きます。田中さんも行きます。(I'm going too. Tanaka's going too. — separately confirmed, additive across sentences/clauses).

## Negative "not... either"
In a negative sentence, も means "not this one either" — very common in daily conversation:

- 私も行きません。— I'm not going either.
- 肉も魚も食べません。— [I] don't eat meat or fish [either]. (see below for the も...も pattern)

## も...も — "both...and" / "neither...nor"
Repeating も across two or more items gives an exhaustive "both X and Y" (affirmative) or "neither X nor Y" (negative):

- 兄も姉もいます。— I have both an older brother and an older sister.
- 時間もお金もない。— [I] have neither time nor money.

This is a distinct, stronger construction from と — と just lists things factually, も...も emphasizes the "even this, even that" completeness.

## Emphatic extremes ("even")
も can push toward "even," especially with numbers or extreme cases:

- 三時間も待ちました。— [I] waited a whopping three hours. (emphasizing it's a lot)
- 一円も持っていない。— [I] don't have even one yen.

## Notes
- も cannot combine with は/が/を on the same noun — it takes their place.
- With other particles (に, で, と, から), も stacks after them rather than replacing them: 東京にも行きました。— [I] went to Tokyo too.
- Don't confuse the additive も (this note) with も as part of 〜てもいい (see the て-form hub in [[0-overview]]) — that's an unrelated grammaticalized use, not "also."

title: よ - asserting new information particle
content:
# よ - asserting new information particle

A sentence-final particle that flags what you're saying as new/important information the listener doesn't have yet — roughly "I'm telling you," "just so you know." See [[6a-ね]] for the contrasting "seeking agreement" particle and [[6c-わ]] for the softening particle.

## Asserting new info
Use よ when you're telling the listener something they likely don't already know, or correcting/updating their assumption:

- もう12時ですよ。— It's already 12, you know. (they probably didn't realize)
- これ、おいしいですよ。— This is tasty, [I'm telling you]. (recommending, they haven't tried it)
- 危ないよ! — Watch out! / That's dangerous! (urgent new info)

Compare directly with ね: おいしいですね (isn't this tasty — inviting agreement, assuming they'll agree) vs おいしいですよ (this is tasty — informing/asserting, they don't know yet).

## Correction / pushback
よ carries a mild "actually..." force when contradicting or correcting the listener:

- 違いますよ。— That's wrong, [actually].
- もう食べましたよ。— [I] already ate, [you know]. (correcting an assumption that you hadn't)

Overusing よ in this mode can come across as pushy or condescending — tone and relationship matter a lot.

## Emphasis / insistence
よ can simply add force/insistence to a statement, opinion, or invitation:

- 行きましょうよ! — Let's go [come on]!
- 大丈夫ですよ。— It's fine, [really].

## Stacking with か/ね
よ combines with other sentence-final particles:

- よね — assert + check agreement: 明日休みですよね? — Tomorrow's a holiday, right? (see [[6a-ね]])
- よ alone doesn't combine with か (they serve opposite functions — asserting vs questioning) — か replaces よ, not stacks with it.

## Notes
- Dial down よ with strangers/superiors in sensitive moments — it can sound blunt; ね or no particle at all is safer when unsure.
- よ is not inherently rude — it's just informational emphasis; tone of voice determines whether it lands as helpful or curt.

title: ね - seeking agreement particle
content:
# ね - seeking agreement particle

A sentence-final particle that invites the listener to confirm, agree, or share the feeling — roughly "right?" / "isn't it?" but far more woven into daily speech than that English gloss suggests. See [[6a-よ]] for the contrasting "new info" particle and [[6c-わ]] for the softening particle.

## Seeking agreement / confirmation
The default use — you believe something and are checking the listener agrees or already knows:

- いい天気ですね。— Nice weather, isn't it?
- これ、おいしいですね。— This is tasty, right?
- 明日休みですよね? — Tomorrow's a day off, right? (よね stacks よ's assertion with ね's checking)

## Softening / inviting connection
Even when there's nothing to literally confirm, ね softens a statement and signals "I'm not just broadcasting at you, I want your reaction":

- 頑張りましたね。— [You] worked hard, huh. (empathetic, not really a question)
- そうですね... — Well, let's see... (used constantly as a thinking filler before answering)

そうですね is worth knowing on its own — it's the single most common way to buy a beat before responding, or to agree ("that's right").

## Turn-taking / conversational glue
ね gets dropped in constantly, especially at clause boundaries in casual speech, functioning almost like "you know" — checking the listener is still following:

- 昨日ね、友達とね、映画を見に行ったんです。— So yesterday, right, with a friend, [I] went to see a movie.

This mid-sentence use is very casual/spoken — don't overuse it in writing or formal speech.

## Notes
- ね can attach after plain or polite forms, and after other sentence-final particles (よね, わね).
- Tone matters a lot: rising/soft ね invites genuine agreement; flatter ね is closer to filler. Pattern-matching from listening is more reliable than a rule here.
- Overusing ね is a common learner tell — natives use it, but not on every single sentence.

title: わ - softening particle
content:
# わ - softening particle

A sentence-final particle that softens a statement, adding a gentle, personal, self-directed feel. See [[6a-ね]] and [[6a-よ]] for the other sentence-final particles it can combine with.

## Softening a statement
わ rounds off a sentence without asserting or demanding anything from the listener — closer to "..." or a soft exhale than an actual grammatical marker:

- 疲れたわ。— [I'm] tired. (soft, musing aloud)
- そうだわ、忘れてた。— Oh right, [I] forgot. (realization, said to oneself)
- 行くわ。— [I]'ll go. (gentle statement of intent)

## Gendered association (softening the reality)
わ is traditionally associated with feminine speech in standard/Tokyo Japanese — women's speech textbooks lean on it heavily. In real usage this has loosened a lot:
- In the Kansai dialect (Osaka/Kyoto etc.), わ is used by everyone regardless of gender, with a flatter, more matter-of-fact tone than the standard-dialect "soft" version.
- In standard-dialect casual speech, men do use わ occasionally, especially rising-intonation わ! for surprise, but it still reads as softer/more feminine than よ or plain assertion.
- Media (anime, drama) exaggerates わ as a "feminine speech" marker far more than real usage — don't calibrate your sense of naturalness from subtitles alone.

## Stacking with よ/ね
わ combines with other sentence-final particles, always coming first:

- 行くわよ。— [I]'ll go, [you know]. (わ softens, よ asserts)
- 疲れたわね。— [I'm] tired, aren't I. (わ softens, ね invites agreement)

## Notes
- Don't over-invest in producing わ yourself early on — it's easy to sound off if the gendered register doesn't match your intent. Recognizing it in speech/media is more useful than actively using it as a learner.
- Distinct from the standalone exclamation わ! (surprise, "whoa!") — same kana, unrelated function, judged from context/intonation.

title: か - question particle
content:
# か - question particle

Turns a statement into a question by attaching to the end. Also does double duty as an "or" connector between choices. See [[6a-ね]]/[[6a-よ]] for the other sentence-final particles it can precede but not stack after.

## Basic yes/no and wh-questions
Add か to the end of a plain or polite sentence to make it a question — no word-order change needed, unlike English:

- 学生ですか。— Are [you] a student?
- 何を食べますか。— What will [you] eat?
- 行きましたか。— Did [you] go?

## Politeness split
か is the standard way to ask questions in polite (です/ます) speech. In casual speech, か is often dropped entirely, replaced by rising intonation alone, or by の (see [[4-の]] "explanatory の"):

- 行きますか。(polite, explicit question marker)
- 行くの? (casual, の + rising tone)
- 行く? (casual, tone alone — か would sound oddly formal/blunt here)

Using plain-form + か in casual speech (行くか?) can sound rough/masculine — worth knowing but not a default beginners should reach for.

## "Or" between choices
か can link two or more nouns/clauses as alternatives:

- コーヒーか紅茶がほしいです。— I want coffee or tea.
- 行くか行かないか決めてください。— Please decide whether to go or not.

## Embedded questions (uncertainty inside a sentence)
か can mark an embedded question — "whether/if" — inside a larger sentence, very common with 分かる/知る/考える:

- 彼が来るかどうか分かりません。— I don't know whether he'll come. (どうか adds "or not")
- 何を食べるか決めていません。— [I] haven't decided what to eat.

This plain-form-plus-か pattern is the backbone of a lot of "I wonder / not sure if" constructions.

## Rhetorical / softening use
か can appear mid-sentence or doubled up to hedge or muse aloud, without being a real question:

- そうですか。— Is that so. / I see. (acknowledging, not actually asking)
- 誰か来ましたか。— Did someone come? (誰か = "someone," か attached to 誰 makes an indefinite pronoun — a different, unrelated job of か)

## Notes
- か replaces nothing — it just attaches to the end of an already-complete sentence.
- か doesn't combine with よ (see [[6a-よ]]) since they point opposite directions (assert vs. ask), but でしょうか is common for a softer, more polite "I wonder/is it perhaps."
- か attached to question words (誰, 何, どこ, いつ) turns them into indefinites: 誰か (someone), 何か (something), どこか (somewhere) — worth recognizing as a separate pattern from the sentence-final question use.

title: たい-form — want to
content:
# たい-form — want to

Turns a verb into "want to [verb]." Built directly from the ます-stem (see [[1-conjugation-group]]), and conjugates like an い-adjective once formed.

## Forming it
ます-stem + たい, for any group:

- 食べる → 食べたい — want to eat
- 飲む → 飲みたい — want to drink
- 行く → 行きたい — want to go
- する → したい — want to do
- 来る (kuru) → 来たい (きたい) — want to come

## Conjugates as an い-adjective, not a verb
Once you've formed X-たい, treat it exactly like an い-adjective (see the adjective notes) — not like a verb:

| | Plain | Polite |
|---|---|---|
| Non-past affirmative | 食べたい | 食べたいです |
| Non-past negative | 食べたくない | 食べたくないです |
| Past affirmative | 食べたかった | 食べたかったです |
| Past negative | 食べたくなかった | 食べたくなかったです |

## Object marking: が vs を
With たい, the object can take either が or を — が leans slightly more natural/common in casual speech, を is common when emphasizing the object or in more neutral/written style:

- 水が飲みたい。/ 水を飲みたい。— [I] want to drink water.

This is the same pattern behind other feeling/desire predicates taking が (see [[1b-が]]) — たい softens but doesn't eliminate that pull toward が.

## First person (and why 3rd person is different)
Plain たい directly describes the *speaker's* own desire — using it to state someone else's desire sounds off, similar to how you can't directly say "he is sad" the same way you say "I am sad" in Japanese:

- 私は行きたいです。— I want to go. (natural)
- ~~彼は行きたいです。~~ — sounds like you're claiming direct access to his inner state.

For third parties, hedge or use different constructions — 彼は行きたがっている (he seems to want to go, たがる form) or 彼は行きたいと言っています (he says he wants to go). These are long-tail refinements; not needed to start using たい for yourself.

## Notes
- たい + と思う stacks constantly in natural speech: 食べたいと思います。— I think I want to eat. (softens the directness of stating a desire, especially in polite contexts)
- Don't confuse verb-stem+たい (want to do) with the unrelated い-adjective 高い/暑い etc. — the たい here is a suffix, not a coincidence of spelling.

title: Potential form (可能形) — ability
content:
# Potential form (可能形) — ability

Turns a verb into "can [verb]" — a single-word alternative to 〜ことができる (see [[0-overview]]'s workhorse list, which pairs the two). Group-dependent, built directly on [[1-conjugation-group]].

## Forming it

**う-verbs (Group 1)** — change the final -u to -e, add る:

- 読む → 読める — can read
- 話す → 話せる — can speak
- 行く → 行ける — can go
- 買う → 買える — can buy

**る-verbs (Group 2)** — drop る, add られる:

- 食べる → 食べられる — can eat
- 見る → 見られる — can see

**Irregulars**
- する → できる — can do
- 来る (kuru) → 来られる (こられる) — can come

The result is always a る-verb (Group 2) regardless of the original group, so it conjugates like 食べる from there: 食べられます, 食べられない, 食べられました, etc.

## The ら抜き言葉 shortcut (colloquial)
In casual speech, る-verb potentials commonly drop the ら: 食べられる → 食べれる, 見られる → 見れる. This is extremely common in spoken Japanese but still considered non-standard/incorrect in formal writing and on tests — recognize it, but default to the full られる form when producing polite or written Japanese.

## Object marking: を → が
Just like たい (see [[4-たい-form]]), potential form pulls the object toward が instead of を — this is the same "feeling/ability predicate" pull as 好き, ほしい, 分かる:

- 日本語を話す → 日本語が話せる。— [I] can speak Japanese.
- 漢字を読む → 漢字が読める。— [I] can read kanji.

を isn't strictly wrong here, but が is the more natural default.

## Potential vs 〜ことができる
Both mean "can do X," but potential form is shorter and more common in speech; ことができる is more common in writing, explanations, or when the verb's potential form would be awkward/ambiguous:

- 泳げます。/ 泳ぐことができます。— [I] can swim. (interchangeable)
- ことができる also works cleanly with する-verbs where できる already exists: 運転することができる vs the more natural 運転できる (する's own potential).

## Potential vs たい — don't confuse the two
たい = want to (desire); potential = can (ability). They stack: 食べられるものを食べたい。— [I] want to eat something [that I] am able to eat.

## Notes
- Potential form describes general capability/possibility, not a one-off achievement — for "I managed to do X [this one time]," other constructions (〜ことができた, context) are often more natural, but potential past (食べられた) is still fine and commonly used.
- Some verbs have a distinct, older potential form for う-verbs using れる (話される) which is actually the passive form — don't confuse conversationally derived 話せる (potential) with 話される (passive/honorific); they look similar but come from different mechanics.

title: Conditionals — たら / ば / と / なら
content:
# Conditionals — たら / ば / と / なら

Japanese has four conditional forms where English just has "if." They overlap heavily but aren't interchangeable. Per [[0-overview]], たら is the one to master first — it's the most flexible and covers casual daily "if/when" almost entirely; treat ば/と/なら as later refinements, not day-one material.

## たら — the default, flexible conditional
Forms off plain past (た-form, see [[2-て-form]] for the sound-shift table) + ら:

- 食べたら → if/when [you] eat
- 高かったら → if [it]'s expensive (い-adjective past + ら)
- 暇だったら → if [I]'m free (な-adjective/noun past + ら)

たら covers one-off hypotheticals, sequences, and suggestions/requests after the fact — this breadth is exactly why it's the safe daily default:

- 雨が降ったら、行きません。— If it rains, [I] won't go.
- 駅に着いたら、電話してください。— When [you] arrive at the station, please call. (sequence: arrive, then call)
- 疲れたら、休んでください。— If/when [you] get tired, please rest.

## と — mechanical/automatic "whenever"
Already covered from the particle side in [[5a-と]] — と-conditional describes something that *always* follows automatically, not a one-off choice. Can't be used for suggestions, requests, or anything involving deliberate will in the result clause:

- 春になると、暖かくなる。— When spring comes, it gets warm. (natural law, always true)
- ~~このボタンを押すと、開けてください。~~ — ungrammatical: と can't end in a request.

## ば — formal/written, "if" with emphasis on the condition itself
Formed by changing the final -u of the plain non-past to -eba (う-verbs) or dropping る and adding れば (る-verbs):

- 読む → 読めば — if [you] read
- 食べる → 食べれば — if [you] eat
- 高い → 高ければ — if [it]'s expensive

ば feels more formal/written than たら, and is common in set phrases and proverbs:

- 聞けば分かります。— If [you] ask, [you]'ll understand.
- すみませんが、できればお願いします。— Sorry, if possible, please [do it]. (できれば is a very common fixed phrase — "if possible")

Like と, ば traditionally resists ending in a direct request/command in the strictest grammar, though this is loosened in casual modern use — たら remains the safer choice when in doubt.

## なら — conditional on a premise/topic, not an event
なら reacts to something already said or assumed — "if that's the case, then..." — and can also mean "if you're going to do X" (advice framing). It attaches to plain form (dropping the copula for nouns/な-adjectives):

- 行くなら、傘を持って行って。— If you're going [to go], take an umbrella. (reacting to their stated plan)
- 田中さんなら、知っていると思います。— If it's [about] Tanaka, I think [he]'d know. (premise: talking about Tanaka specifically)

なら is distinct from the other three because it's not really about a hypothetical event unfolding — it's about responding to a premise on the table.

## Quick comparison

| Form | Best for | Can end in request/command? |
|---|---|---|
| たら | Default, flexible, sequences | Yes |
| と | Automatic/mechanical results | No |
| ば | Formal, written, set phrases | Traditionally no (loosening) |
| なら | Reacting to a stated premise/plan | Yes |

## Notes
- All four can often be swapped for たら without sounding wrong in casual speech — the finer distinctions matter more for natural-sounding formal/written Japanese than for getting understood.
- Don't drill ば/と/なら hard until たら is automatic — per [[0-overview]], this is explicitly long-tail refinement once the workhorse form is solid.

title: Volitional form — let's / I intend to
content:
# Volitional form — let's / I intend to

Expresses "let's [do]" (inviting someone) or "I will/intend to [do]" (stating your own resolve). Has both polite and plain registers, mirroring [[3-plain-vs-polite-form]].

## Polite volitional — ましょう
ます-stem (see [[1-conjugation-group]]) + ましょう:

- 食べる → 食べましょう — let's eat
- 行く → 行きましょう — let's go
- する → しましょう — let's do [it]

ましょうか softens it into a suggestion/offer rather than a direct proposal:

- 手伝いましょうか。— Shall [I] help?
- 一緒に行きましょうか。— Shall we go together?

## Plain volitional — group-dependent sound shift
**う-verbs**: change final -u to -o, add う:
- 行く → 行こう — let's go / I'll go
- 話す → 話そう — let's talk
- 買う → 買おう — let's buy

**る-verbs**: drop る, add よう:
- 食べる → 食べよう — let's eat
- 見る → 見よう — let's watch

**Irregulars**: する → しよう, 来る (kuru) → 来よう (こよう)

## Two readings: "let's" vs "I will"
Context (especially the presence of a listener to invite) decides which reading applies — the form itself doesn't distinguish:

- さあ、食べよう! — Alright, let's eat! (inviting)
- 明日から頑張ろうと思う。— I think I'll work hard starting tomorrow. (self-directed resolve, often paired with と思う — see [[5a-と]])

The self-directed "I will" reading pairs constantly with 〜と思う to soften a bare declaration of intent into "I'm thinking I'll...":

- 留学しようと思っています。— I'm thinking of studying abroad.

## Volitional vs たい vs plain future
Don't confuse these three, which all touch "future/intent" territory:

- 食べたい — want to eat (desire, not commitment)
- 食べよう — let's eat / I will eat (invitation or resolve)
- 食べる — will eat (plain non-past also covers simple future, no special "intent" nuance — 明日食べる just states a fact about tomorrow)

## Notes
- Volitional form + とする means "try to (about to)": 帰ろうとしたら、雨が降ってきた。— Just as [I] was about to head home, it started raining.
- ましょう said to someone senior/a stranger out of the blue can sound presumptuous (it implies you're both doing it together) — 〜ませんか (won't you...?) is often a politer way to propose the same thing: 一緒に行きませんか。— Won't [you] go with [me]?

title: あげる / くれる / もらう — giving and receiving
content:
# あげる / くれる / もらう — giving and receiving

Three verbs for "give/receive," but the choice isn't about who physically hands what to whom — it's about **direction relative to the speaker's in-group**, and getting it backwards is a common, noticeable learner mistake. Core per [[0-overview]].

## The three verbs

**あげる** — I/someone give to someone else (away from the speaker's perspective)
**くれる** — someone gives to me/my in-group (toward the speaker's perspective)
**もらう** — I/someone receive from someone else (receiving, direction-neutral on the giving side)

The key mental model: あげる and くれる both mean "give," but あげる is used when the giving moves *away* from you (you→someone, or A→B where you're not involved), while くれる is used when the giving moves *toward* you (someone→you). もらう flips the frame entirely — it's from the receiver's viewpoint regardless of direction.

## あげる — giving away from yourself
- 私は友達にプレゼントをあげました。— I gave my friend a present.
- 田中さんは山田さんに本をあげました。— Tanaka gave Yamada a book. (neither party is "me," but the giving is described from the giver's side, away from them)

Using あげる for something given *to you* sounds off — 友達は私にプレゼントをあげました is grammatically parseable but unnatural; native speakers reach for くれる instead.

## くれる — giving toward yourself (or your in-group)
- 友達が私にプレゼントをくれました。— My friend gave me a present.
- 田中さんが弟にお金をくれました。— Tanaka gave my little brother money. (in-group extends to family/close circle, not just literal "me")

The giver takes が (not は as topic, typically — が marks who's doing the giving, since the interesting/new info is often who gave it):

- 誰がくれたの? — Who gave [it to you]?

## もらう — receiving (viewpoint flip)
Structured as [receiver]は[giver]に/から[thing]をもらう — receiver is the topic/subject, giver marked with に or から:

- 私は友達にプレゼントをもらいました。— I received a present from my friend. (= my friend gave me a present, same event as the くれる example above, opposite grammatical framing)
- 誕生日に何をもらいましたか。— What did [you] get for your birthday?

あげる/くれる describe the event from the giver's side; もらう describes the same event from the receiver's side — often either works for the same real-world event, and the choice is about whose perspective you want to center.

## Quick decision table

| Direction | Verb | Giver marked with | Topic/subject |
|---|---|---|---|
| Me → someone else | あげる | は/が (giver = topic) | giver |
| Someone → me | くれる | が (giver) | giver, but centers on me as recipient |
| I receive from someone | もらう | に/から (giver) | receiver (me) is topic |

## て-form attachment: favors, not just objects
These three attach to て-form to describe doing an action *as a favor*, not just handing over a thing — this is extremely common in daily speech (see [[2-て-form]]):

- 手伝ってあげる。— I'll help [you] [as a favor, from me outward].
- 手伝ってくれる? — Will [you] help me [as a favor toward me]? (a very common, natural way to ask for help)
- 先生に教えてもらいました。— [I] had the teacher explain [it] [to me]. / The teacher explained it for me.

てくれる and てもらう both describe someone doing something that benefits you, but with different subjects: 教えてくれる (the teacher is the subject, doing it toward me) vs 教えてもらう (I'm the subject, receiving the favor).

## Notes
- あげる toward a social superior can sound presumptuous/condescending (implies you're bestowing something) — さしあげる is the humble alternative in formal contexts; not needed for casual daily use, just good to recognize.
- くれる is the one learners most often get backwards early on, since English "give" doesn't grammaticalize this directional split — if in doubt, ask "did this benefit *me*?" → くれる/もらう territory, not あげる.

title: ている — progressive vs. resultant state
content:
# ている — progressive vs. resultant state

て-form + いる (see [[2-て-form]]) is introduced early as "-ing," but it actually covers two different meanings depending on the verb — mixing them up is a common source of confusion in daily conversation.

## Forming it
Standard て-form attachment: 食べて + いる → 食べている. Conjugates as a る-verb from there:

- 食べている / 食べていない / 食べていた / 食べていなかった
- Polite: 食べています / 食べていません / 食べていました

Casual speech routinely drops the い: 食べてる, 食べてない — extremely common, safe to use casually, but keep the full いる form in polite/written contexts.

## Reading 1 — progressive (action in progress)
With **continuous/durative verbs** (actions that take time to complete), ている describes the action happening right now, mid-way through:

- 今、ご飯を食べている。— [I]'m eating right now.
- 雨が降っている。— It's raining. (ongoing)
- 本を読んでいます。— [I]'m reading a book.

This is the "-ing" reading most learners default to — correct for this class of verbs.

## Reading 2 — resultant state (the result of a change persists)
With **instantaneous/punctual verbs** (actions that happen in a single moment, not drawn out — 死ぬ, 結婚する, 知る, 落ちる, 開く), ている instead describes the *state that results* from that instant having already happened:

- 結婚している。— [I]'m married. (NOT "I'm in the middle of marrying" — the event already happened, and the resulting state persists)
- 知っている。— [I] know. (the moment of learning already happened; knowing is the resulting state)
- 窓が開いている。— The window is open. (someone opened it; open is the resulting state)
- 彼は死んでいる。— He is dead. (not "he is dying")

This trips learners up specifically because English "-ing" would suggest the action is mid-way, but for these verbs Japanese ている always means the state-after-the-fact, never "in the process of."

## How to tell which reading applies
Ask whether the verb describes something that takes a stretch of time (progressive reading) or something that happens in an instant, after which a new state holds (resultant-state reading). A few genuinely ambiguous verbs (着る — to wear/put on) can go either way and need context:

- 今、服を着ている。— [I]'m putting on clothes. (in progress) OR [I]'m wearing clothes. (state) — both readings exist; context/tone disambiguates.

## ている vs てある
てある is related but distinct — it marks a deliberately-arranged resultant state, usually of something someone did on purpose to an object, and implies the state was set up intentionally (often for a purpose):

- 窓が開いている。— The window is open. (neutral observation of a state)
- 窓が開けてある。— The window has been [deliberately] left open. (implies someone did it on purpose, often "in preparation for something" — see て + おく in [[2-て-form]], which is the deliberate-preparation act; てある is the resulting state of that act)

てある is lower-frequency in casual daily talk than ている — recognize it, but ている does most of the daily work.

## Notes
- 知る is a common trap: 知る itself means "to learn/find out" (a moment), so "I know" is always 知っている, never the bare plain-form 知る in the present-state sense — 知りません (I don't know) is the one common exception where the plain negative works directly without ている.
- Habitual/repeated actions can also use ている: 毎日走っている。— [I] run every day. (a third loose use, close to "I habitually do X," distinct from both readings above but easy to fold into the "ongoing state" intuition once you're comfortable with the core two.)

title: たり〜たりする - listing representative actions
content:
# たり〜たりする - listing representative actions

Lists a few example actions out of a larger, unstated set — "[I do] things like X and Y," not an exhaustive account of everything that happens. Built on the same sound-shift as plain past (た-form, see [[2-て-form]]), just with り attached.

## Forming it
Plain past (た-form) + り, repeated for each example action, ending in する (conjugated for tense/register):

- 休みの日は本を読んだり、映画を見たりします。— On days off, [I] do things like read books and watch movies.
- 週末は掃除したり、洗濯したりします。— On weekends, [I] do things like clean and do laundry.
- 公園で走ったり、散歩したりしました。— At the park, [I] did things like run and take walks.

The final する carries the actual tense/politeness — the individual たり verbs themselves don't need to match tense with each other or with する.

## Why not just use て-form or と for the list?
Compare to plain て-form sequencing (see [[2-て-form]]) or と's exhaustive "and" (see [[../1-particle/5a-と]]):

- 本を読んで、映画を見ました。— [I] read a book, [then] watched a movie. (て-form: a complete, sequential account of exactly what happened)
- 本を読んだり、映画を見たりしました。— [I] did things like read a book and watch a movie. (たり: examples from a longer, unstated list — implies other things happened too)

たり is the natural choice whenever you're giving a representative sample rather than a complete report — which covers a huge share of daily "what do you do on weekends" type conversation.

## Contradictory/alternating actions
たり also works well for describing back-and-forth or contradictory actions, emphasizing the alternation itself:

- 天気は良かったり悪かったりです。— The weather is sometimes good, sometimes bad.
- 行ったり来たりする。— [To] go back and forth. (a common fixed expression, lit. "going and coming")

## Single たり (less common, but valid)
たり can technically appear just once, still implying "among other things," though doubling it is far more natural and common in daily speech:

- テレビを見たりして、ゆっくりしました。— [I] relaxed, [doing things] like watching TV [among other things].

## Notes
- Don't confuse たり (listing representative/alternating actions) with たら (conditional, see [[6-conditional]]) — both come from the same た-stem sound-shift, but たり always needs する at the end and never means "if/when."
- Extremely common when answering casual "what do you usually do" questions — a natural, idiomatic way to avoid listing an exhaustive, overly precise account of your routine.

title: い-adjective vs な-adjective
content:
# い-adjective vs な-adjective

Japanese adjectives split into two structurally different types. Telling them apart matters because they conjugate completely differently — い-adjectives conjugate on their own, な-adjectives lean on the copula だ/です just like nouns (see [[3-plain-vs-polite-form]] in 2-verb).

## Identifying the two types

**い-adjectives** — end in い in dictionary form (with a few exceptions below), conjugate independently:

- 高い (takai) — expensive/tall
- 暑い (atsui) — hot
- おいしい (oishii) — tasty
- いい (ii) / 良い (yoi) — good (irregular, see below)

**な-adjectives** — don't end in a "real" い (or do, but aren't true い-adjectives — see the trap below), require な before a noun and だ/です for predicate use, behave grammatically like nouns:

- 静か(な) — quiet
- 元気(な) — energetic/well
- きれい(な) — pretty/clean
- 有名(な) — famous
- 好き(な) — liked/favorite (note: きれい and 嫌い/好き end in い but are な-adjectives — the trap below)

## The い-adjective trap
A handful of words end in -い but are actually な-adjectives — memorize these as exceptions:

- きれい(な) — pretty (not きれ + い)
- 嫌い(な) — disliked
- 有名(な) is safe (doesn't end in い) but きらい/きれい specifically are the classic gotchas.

Test: try dropping the い and conjugating as an い-adjective (静かい→静かくない). If that sounds wrong and you'd naturally reach for だ/です instead, it's な.

## い-adjective conjugation
Conjugates without needing だ/です at all in plain form:

| | Plain | Polite |
|---|---|---|
| Non-past affirmative | 高い | 高いです |
| Non-past negative | 高くない | 高くないです / 高くありません |
| Past affirmative | 高かった | 高かったです |
| Past negative | 高くなかった | 高くなかったです |

Pattern: drop い, then -くない (negative), -かった (past), -くなかった (past negative). This shift (い→く/かった) is worth drilling the same way the て-form sound shifts are.

## な-adjective conjugation
Conjugates exactly like a noun + copula (だ/です) — see the copula table in [[3-plain-vs-polite-form]]:

| | Plain | Polite |
|---|---|---|
| Non-past affirmative | 静かだ | 静かです |
| Non-past negative | 静かじゃない | 静かじゃないです / 静かではありません |
| Past affirmative | 静かだった | 静かでした |
| Past negative | 静かじゃなかった | 静かじゃなかったです |

## Modifying a noun (attributive use)
This is where the two types visibly diverge in name:

- い-adjective + noun: nothing extra needed — 高い本 (expensive book)
- な-adjective + な + noun: な is required — 静かな部屋 (quiet room), not 静か部屋

Dropping な before a noun is one of the most common beginner mistakes with な-adjectives.

## いい — the one irregular い-adjective
いい (good) conjugates using its older form 良い (よい) for everything except the plain non-past affirmative:

- いい (not いくない for negative)
- 良くない (よくない) — not good
- 良かった (よかった) — was good / thank goodness
- 良くなかった (よくなかった) — was not good

良かった as a standalone exclamation ("thank goodness," "glad [that happened]") is extremely common in daily speech — worth knowing on its own.

## Notes
- Both types can be nominalized/turned adverbial — see [[2-adverbial-form]].
- な-adjectives are sometimes listed in dictionaries without な (静か, 元気) since な itself isn't part of the word — only added when directly modifying a noun.

title: Adverbial form — turning adjectives into adverbs
content:
# Adverbial form — turning adjectives into adverbs

Turns "expensive/quiet" into "expensively/quietly" — modifying a verb instead of a noun. Small, mechanical rule, but used constantly in daily speech (早く来て! — come quickly!). Builds on the い/な split in [[1-i-vs-na-adjective]].

## い-adjectives: い → く
Drop the final い, add く:

- 早い → 早く — early/quickly: 早く起きた。— [I] got up early.
- 高い → 高く — expensively: 高く売れた。— [It] sold for a lot.
- おいしい → おいしく: おいしく作る。— [To] make [it] tasty.

This is the exact same い→く shift used in negative conjugation (高くない, see [[1-i-vs-na-adjective]]) — the adverbial form is just that shift without ない attached.

## な-adjectives: な → に
Drop な, add に:

- 静か(な) → 静かに — quietly: 静かに話してください。— Please speak quietly.
- 上手(な) → 上手に — skillfully: 上手に歌う。— [To] sing well.
- きれい(な) → きれいに: きれいに片付けた。— [I] cleaned [it] up nicely.

## Common daily uses

**Modifying how an action is done** (the core use):
- 元気に育つ。— [To] grow up healthy/energetic.
- 楽しく過ごしてください。— Please have a good/enjoyable time. (楽しい→楽しく)

**With なる (to become)** — extremely common pattern, "become [adjective]":
- 寒くなる。— [It]'s getting cold. (寒い→寒く+なる)
- 静かになる。— [It]'s becoming quiet. (静か+に+なる)
- 上手になりました。— [I] got good at [it].

This adjective+adverbial-form+なる pattern is one of the highest-frequency ways to talk about change in daily conversation — worth internalizing alongside the raw conjugation rule.

**With する (to make/do)** — "make [something adjective]":
- 部屋をきれいにする。— [To] make the room clean/tidy [it] up.
- 声を大きくしてください。— Please make [your] voice louder. (大きい→大きく)

Mirrors なる: なる = something becomes X on its own, する = someone actively makes something X.

## Notes
- いい's adverbial form uses the irregular よく (from 良い), not いく — 仲良く (get along well), よく食べる (eat a lot/often).
- The adverbial form of a な-adjective (Xに) looks identical to the destination/time particle に (see [[3a-に]] in 1-particle) — they're unrelated grammatically, just a coincidence of spelling; context makes it obvious which is which.

title: Comparison — もっと / より / 一番
content:
# Comparison — もっと / より / 一番

Japanese doesn't conjugate adjectives for comparison (no "-er"/"-est" equivalent) — comparison is done with separate words layered on top of the plain adjective from [[1-i-vs-na-adjective]].

## より — "more than" (the comparison particle)
より marks what something is being compared against — attaches after the noun being compared to:

- 今日は昨日より暑いです。— Today is hotter than yesterday. (attached to 昨日, the thing compared against)
- 電車はバスより速い。— The train is faster than the bus.
- これはそれよりいいです。— This is better than that.

The compared item doesn't need を/は/が — より takes its place as the marker on the "than X" side.

## もっと — "more" (intensifier, no explicit comparison target)
もっと boosts a quality without necessarily naming what it's being compared to — "more," "even more":

- もっと大きいのがほしい。— [I] want a bigger one. (bigger [than what I have], target implied not stated)
- もっと頑張ってください。— Please try harder [than you are now].
- もっと静かにしてください。— Please be quieter.

もっと and より can combine: これはそれよりもっといい。— This is even better than that. (more emphatic layering)

## 一番 — "the most" (superlative)
一番 (literally "number one") marks the top of a group — Japan's equivalent of "-est":

- この中で一番好きです。— [I] like [this one] the most out of these.
- 富士山は日本で一番高い山です。— Mt. Fuji is the tallest mountain in Japan.
- 一番好きな食べ物は何ですか。— What's [your] favorite (most-liked) food?

一番 typically pairs with で to mark the group/category being compared within: [category]で一番[adjective].

## Asking "which is more...?"
どちら/どっち (which of two) + が + adjective + ですか is the standard comparison question:

- コーヒーと紅茶とどちらが好きですか。— Which do [you] like more, coffee or tea?
- どっちが安い? — Which one's cheaper? (casual)

For three or more options, どれ (which, of three+) replaces どちら:

- この中でどれが一番おいしいですか。— Which one [of these] is the tastiest?

## Equal comparison — 〜と同じくらい
"As X as Y" / "about the same as":

- 兄は父と同じくらい背が高い。— [My] older brother is about as tall as [my] father.

## Quick reference

| Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|
| AはBより[adj] | A is more [adj] than B |
| もっと[adj] | more [adj] (no explicit target) |
| [category]で一番[adj] | the most [adj] in [category] |
| AとBとどちらが[adj]ですか | which is more [adj], A or B? |
| Aと同じくらい[adj] | as [adj] as A |

## Notes
- より on its own (without もっと) is the neutral, common way to compare two things — don't feel like you need もっと every time; もっと is for emphasis or when there's no explicit "than X" target in the sentence.
- な-adjectives and い-adjectives both slot into these patterns exactly as their plain form — no special comparison conjugation to learn beyond what's already in [[1-i-vs-na-adjective]].

title: んです / んだ - explanatory nuance
content:
# んです / んだ - explanatory nuance

Adds an "explaining/seeking explanation" undertone to a sentence — signals "here's the reason/context," or asks "what's the story here?" Extremely common in natural spoken Japanese despite being rarely taught early. んです is the polite register, んだ the plain/casual register (see [[3-plain-vs-polite-form]] in 2-verb). Built on plain form + の (see [[4-の]] in 1-particle, "explanatory の"), contracted to ん.

## Forming it
Attaches to the plain form of verbs/adjectives, and to noun/な-adjective + な (not だ) before んです:

- 食べる → 食べるんです / 食べるんだ
- 食べた → 食べたんです / 食べたんだ
- 忙しい → 忙しいんです / 忙しいんだ
- 学生 → 学生なんです / 学生なんだ (な inserted before ん for nouns/な-adjectives — unlike plain だ, which is dropped here)

## Explaining a situation (giving background/reason)
The core use: framing a statement as background context or a reason for something, rather than a flat, isolated fact:

- 疲れたんです。— [The thing is,] I'm tired. (explaining why you look tired, or why you're asking to leave early)
- 電車に乗り遅れたんです。— [I'm explaining:] I missed the train. (as opposed to bare 電車に乗り遅れました, which just states the fact with no implied connection to anything)

Compare: 疲れました is a neutral statement. 疲れたんです implies "and that's relevant to what's going on / why I'm telling you this."

## Seeking an explanation (question form)
んですか asks "what's the story?" — genuinely curious, more probing than a bare か-question:

- どうしたんですか。— What's wrong? / What happened? (noticing something's off, asking for the story)
- 何を見ているんですか。— What are [you] looking at? (curious about something already observed, not a cold opening question)

Compare: 何を見ますか (a neutral, out-of-nowhere question about future viewing) vs 何を見ているんですか (noticing someone is currently looking at something, asking about it).

## Softening a request or opinion (with けど/が)
んです pairs constantly with the softening けど/が (see [[12-けど]] in 1-particle) to lead into a request or opinion gently, without stating it too bluntly:

- ちょっと聞きたいんですけど。— [I] wanted to ask something... (leads into a question softly)
- これ、いいと思うんですが。— I think this is good, but... (offering an opinion, leaving room for pushback)

## Casual んだ
Plain-register んだ works identically, just less formal — extremely common in casual conversation, inner monologue, and casual writing:

- そうなんだ! — Oh, I see! / Really! (a very common reaction to new information)
- 疲れたんだ。— [Explaining, casually:] I'm tired.

そうなんだ/そうなんですね are near-automatic reactions in casual/polite conversation respectively — worth having ready as reflexes.

## Notes
- Overusing んです on every sentence sounds unnatural — it's for when there's genuinely some explanation, context, or noticing involved, not a default sentence-ender.
- んです often gets contracted further in very casual speech to just んだ or even dropped to plain の (see [[4-の]] in 1-particle) — all closely related, same underlying mechanic.

title: Requests — て / てください / ないでください / お願いします
content:
# Requests — て / てください / ないでください / お願いします

How to ask someone to do something, or ask them *not* to — a survival-essential set of patterns, all built on て-form (see [[2-て-form]] in 2-verb), plus お願いします for requesting things rather than actions.

## Casual request — bare て-form
Just the て-form on its own, often with rising intonation, works as a soft casual request or instruction between friends/family:

- ちょっと待って。— Wait a sec.
- これ、取って。— Grab that [for me].
- 手伝って! — Help [me]!

This is not rude — it's the normal way to ask close friends/family for small things. It would sound too blunt with strangers or superiors, where てください or further softening is expected.

## Polite request — てください
The standard, safe polite request — works in most everyday polite situations (asking a stranger, service staff, coworkers):

- ちょっと待ってください。— Please wait a moment.
- こちらに来てください。— Please come this way.
- もう一度言ってください。— Please say that again.

てください can still sound like a direct instruction in some contexts (closer to "please do X" as a directive) — for a softer, more deferential request (especially to someone senior or in a formal setting), see the ていただけますか note below.

## Negative request — ないでください
"Please don't [do X]" — built on the plain negative (see [[3-plain-vs-polite-form]] in 2-verb) + でください:

- 写真を撮らないでください。— Please don't take photos.
- ここに座らないでください。— Please don't sit here.
- 心配しないでください。— Please don't worry.

Casually, just ないで on its own (dropping ください) works among friends:

- 心配しないで。— Don't worry. (softer, no explicit ください needed)
- 行かないで! — Don't go!

## お願いします — requesting a thing/service, not an action
Where てください attaches to a *verb* ("please do X"), お願いします attaches to a *noun* — "please [handle/give me] X." Standard for ordering, requesting items, or asking for a service:

- 水をお願いします。— Water, please.
- 会計をお願いします。— The check, please.
- 予約をお願いします。— [I'd like to] make a reservation, please.

For simple physical items, ください and お願いします overlap and are roughly interchangeable — 水をください and 水をお願いします both work, with お願いします feeling a shade more polite/service-oriented:

- 水をください。— [Give me] water, please. (direct, request for the object itself)
- 水をお願いします。— Water, please. (slightly softer/more formal framing, common when ordering)

## お願いします standing alone
Unlike ください, お願いします can stand completely alone, without a preceding verb or even a noun — used when the request is already obvious from context, or as a general "please [take care of this]":

- (handing over a form) お願いします。— Here you go, please [handle this]. / Please [take care of it].
- こちらへどうぞ。— Right this way. / (客) お願いします。— (customer, following) Thank you / please [lead the way].

## よろしくお願いします — the essential set phrase
お願いします is the base of よろしくお願いします, one of the most common phrases in Japanese daily life — said when starting a working relationship, asking a favor, or closing an introduction. It has no direct English equivalent and no ください counterpart:

- はじめまして、よろしくお願いします。— Nice to meet you, [I look forward to working with you / please treat me well].
- 今日はよろしくお願いします。— [Let's do our best] today. (said before a meeting, lesson, collaborative task)

## More polite / deferential requests
For situations calling for extra politeness (asking a favor of someone senior, a customer-facing request, formal writing), てもらえますか or ていただけますか are common upgrades from てください — literally asking "could I receive the favor of your doing X?" (see [[8-giving-receiving]] in 2-verb for the もらう mechanic behind this):

- 手伝ってもらえますか。— Could [you] help me? (fairly polite)
- もう少し待っていただけますか。— Could [you] wait a bit longer? (more formal/deferential)

These read as questions asking permission/favor rather than direct commands, which is why they land as more polite than a bare てください.

## Quick ladder (casual → most polite)

| Form | Register | Attaches to |
|---|---|---|
| 〜て | Casual, close friends/family | verb |
| 〜てください | Standard polite, safe default | verb |
| 〜てもらえますか | Polite, asking a favor | verb |
| 〜ていただけますか | Formal/deferential | verb |
| Xをお願いします | Standard polite, ordering/requesting items | noun |

Negative mirrors the same ladder: 〜ないで (casual) → 〜ないでください (polite).

## Notes
- てください directed at a stranger out of nowhere for something non-obvious can sound like an order — pairing with すみません or a softening んですが (see [[1-んです]]) makes it land more naturally: すみません、写真を撮ってもらえますか。— Excuse me, could [you] take a photo [for me]?
- Don't confuse ないでください (please don't do X) with なくてもいい (don't have to / it's fine not to do X, the negative counterpart of permission てもいい) — different meanings, easy to mix up at a glance.

title: Obligation — 〜なければならない / 〜なくちゃ / 〜なきゃ
content:
# Obligation — 〜なければならない / 〜なくちゃ / 〜なきゃ

"Have to / must [do X]" — built from the plain negative (see [[3-plain-vs-polite-form]] in 2-verb) plus a conditional-shaped ending. Several versions exist on a formality spectrum from stiff/written to very casual.

## The underlying logic
All versions share the same shape: [plain negative stem]く + a conditional ending ("if [you] don't do X..."), with the rest ("...it's no good / won't do") dropped or contracted. Literally "if [you] don't do X, [it's bad]" → practically "[you] have to do X."

## Formal/written: 〜なければならない
ない-form, drop い, add ければならない:

- 行く → 行かない → 行かなければならない — [I] have to go.
- 食べる → 食べない → 食べなければならない — [I] have to eat.
- する → しない → しなければならない — [I] have to do [it].

This is the full, formal version — common in writing, announcements, rules. A bit stiff for casual daily speech but not wrong.

## Slightly softer/common: 〜なくてはいけない
Same idea, different conditional ending (なくては instead of なければ), also fairly common in both speech and writing:

- 行かなくてはいけない — [I] have to go.
- 食べなくてはいけない — [I] have to eat.

なければならない and なくてはいけない are largely interchangeable in daily use — pick whichever comes to mind.

## Casual contraction: 〜なくちゃ
なくては contracts to なくちゃ in casual speech — the ending (いけない) is very often dropped entirely, since the obligation is understood from なくちゃ alone:

- 行かなくちゃ(いけない)。— [I] gotta go.
- もう寝なくちゃ。— [I] gotta sleep now.

Dropping いけない and just ending on なくちゃ is extremely natural and common — a bare なくちゃ! by itself (e.g. glancing at a clock) reads as "gotta go/gotta do it."

## Most casual contraction: 〜なきゃ
なければ contracts to なきゃ — same deal, いけない/ならない routinely dropped:

- 行かなきゃ(ならない)。— [I] gotta go.
- 早く起きなきゃ。— [I] have to get up early.

なきゃ is probably the single most common way "have to" gets expressed in relaxed daily conversation — more casual-sounding than なくちゃ to most ears, though both are fine.

## Quick formality reference

| Form | Register |
|---|---|
| 〜なければならない | Formal/written |
| 〜なくてはいけない | Neutral/common |
| 〜なくちゃ(いけない) | Casual, contraction of なくては |
| 〜なきゃ(ならない) | Very casual, contraction of なければ |

## Notes
- All of these attach to the plain negative stem — the group-dependent negative conjugation rules from [[1-conjugation-group]] (2-verb) apply first, before adding these endings.
- 〜なきゃ/なくちゃ standing completely alone (no verb before it, no いけない after) is a common standalone reaction meaning "I should get going" or "gotta do that [thing we were just discussing]" — context fills in the rest.

title: ちゃう / じゃう - casual contraction of てしまう
content:
# ちゃう / じゃう - casual contraction of てしまう

Casual, contracted form of て-form + しまう (see [[2-て-form]] in 2-verb). てしまう itself means "end up doing," "finish doing completely," or "do something regrettable" — ちゃう is how that sounds in relaxed daily speech, and it's everywhere in real conversation.

## How the contraction works
て + しまう → ちゃう (for verbs whose て-form ends in て). で + しまう → じゃう (for verbs whose て-form ends in で, i.e. the んで group — see the sound-shift table in [[2-て-form]]):

- 食べてしまう → 食べちゃう — end up eating / eat it all
- 忘れてしまう → 忘れちゃう — end up forgetting
- 読んでしまう → 読んじゃう — end up reading / finish reading (で→じゃう)
- 死んでしまう → 死んじゃう — end up dying

Conjugates as a regular う-verb from there: ちゃう/ちゃった/ちゃわない, じゃう/じゃった/じゃわない.

## Two core meanings (same as full てしまう)

**Completion — did something fully/entirely:**
- もう食べちゃった。— [I] already finished eating (all of it).
- 全部読んじゃった。— [I] read the whole thing.

**Regret / unintended consequence — something happened that you wish hadn't, often accidentally:**
- 財布を忘れちゃった。— [I] went and forgot my wallet. (oops)
- 壊しちゃった。— [I] broke it. (accidentally, and feeling bad about it)
- 寝ちゃった。— [I] [accidentally] fell asleep. (e.g. when you meant to stay awake)

Which reading applies is mostly determined by context — a completion-type verb with no obvious downside (食べちゃう) reads as "finished eating"; an accident-prone context (忘れちゃう, 壊しちゃう) reads as regret.

## Very common standalone reactions
- やっちゃった! — [I] [screwed up and] did it! / Oh no, I did the thing [again]. (very common exclamation after a small mistake)
- しちゃった。— [I] did it [without meaning to] / [I] went ahead and did it.

## Politeness note
ちゃう/じゃう is casual-register only — for polite speech, use the full てしまいます/てしまいました, or drop the nuance and just use a plain verb if the "regret/completion" flavor isn't essential to convey.

## Notes
- Don't confuse the contraction ちゃう with random verbs that happen to end in ちゃう unrelatedly — in practice this is rare, context makes it obvious.
- Casual speech often further contracts the past tense: ちゃった is already the norm; you won't typically see it shortened further, but you will hear it constantly in fast, natural speech (やっちゃった、忘れちゃった、寝ちゃった are all near-reflexive daily phrases).

title: そう / みたい / らしい - appearance, seeming, hearsay
content:
# そう / みたい / らしい - appearance, seeming, hearsay

Three ways to say "looks like / seems / apparently," each with a distinct source of information: そう is a visual/sensory impression, みたい is a casual, general "seems like," and らしい is hearsay/what you heard secondhand. Mixing these up is a common source of subtle unnaturalness even at intermediate level.

## そう (様態) — visual/sensory impression, "looks like"
Attaches to the ます-stem of verbs (see [[1-conjugation-group]] in 2-verb) or the stem of い/な-adjectives (drop the final い or な), describing an impression formed by looking at something — before you've confirmed it:

- おいしそう。— [That] looks tasty. (haven't tasted it yet, judging by appearance)
- 雨が降りそう。— [It] looks like [it]'s about to rain. (based on the sky right now)
- 疲れてそう。— [You] look tired. (visual impression)
- 便利そう。— [That] looks convenient. (な-adjective stem, drop な: 便利(な)→便利そう)

Irregular: いい → よさそう (not いいそう), ない → なさそう.

This そう is about a *prediction/impression from what you currently perceive* — it's specifically not for something you've already confirmed as true (for that, just state it directly: おいしいです, not おいしいそうです in that sense — see hearsay そう below for the confusingly identical-looking but different construction).

## そう (伝聞) — hearsay, "I heard that" (different grammar, same word!)
A second, unrelated そう attaches to the **full plain form** (not the stem) and means "I heard that..." — reporting something you were told, not your own impression:

- 明日は雨が降るそうです。— I heard [it]'ll rain tomorrow. (from the news, someone else, etc.)
- 田中さんは忙しいそうです。— I heard Tanaka is busy.

The difference is entirely in what そう attaches to: stem (降りそう, appearance) vs. full plain form (降るそうです, hearsay) — easy to mix up, worth double-checking which one you mean.

## みたい — casual "seems like" (general-purpose, spoken)
The casual, catch-all version of both そう and らしい — attaches after the plain form of verbs/い-adjectives, or directly after nouns/な-adjective stems (no な needed before みたい):

- 雨みたい。— Seems like rain. (could be visual, could be secondhand — みたい doesn't specify the source)
- 元気みたい。— [They] seem energetic/well.
- 学生みたいです。— [They] seem to be a student.

みたい is the natural default in casual conversation when you don't need to be precise about *why* you think something — much more common in speech than carefully choosing between visual-そう and hearsay-そう.

## らしい — hearsay / "apparently" (also: "typical of")
Similar to hearsay-そう, but slightly more distanced/uncertain in tone, and also carries a secondary "typical of X" meaning. Attaches after plain form (with the same noun/な-adjective exception as みたい — no だ needed):

- 明日は雨らしい。— Apparently [it]'ll rain tomorrow. (secondhand, slightly more hedge than そう)
- 彼は忙しいらしいです。— [I hear] he's busy.
- 子供らしい。— [That]'s childlike / typical of a child. (the "typical of" sense — distinct usage, worth recognizing)

## Quick comparison

| Form | Attaches to | Source of info |
|---|---|---|
| Xそう (appearance) | verb/adjective stem | visual impression, before confirming |
| Xそうです (hearsay) | full plain form | reported, "I heard" |
| Xみたい | plain form / noun | casual, source unspecified — safest default |
| Xらしい | plain form / noun | hearsay, more distanced; also "typical of" |

## Notes
- In casual daily conversation, みたい does most of the work — don't stress over precisely choosing between visual-そう and らしい early on.
- All four can stack with んです/けど for softening (see [[1-んです]]): 雨が降りそうなんですけど。— It looks like it might rain, so...

title: すぎる - "too much"
content:
# すぎる - "too much"

Attaches to verbs or adjectives to say something is excessive — "too [X]," "[verb] too much." Extremely common in daily complaints, observations, and self-deprecating remarks.

## Forming it

**With verbs** — ます-stem (see [[1-conjugation-group]] in 2-verb) + すぎる:

- 食べる → 食べすぎる — eat too much
- 飲む → 飲みすぎる — drink too much
- 働く → 働きすぎる — work too much
- 寝る → 寝すぎる — sleep too much

**With い-adjectives** — drop the final い, add すぎる:

- 高い → 高すぎる — too expensive
- 難しい → 難しすぎる — too difficult
- 忙しい → 忙しすぎる — too busy

**With な-adjectives** — drop な, add すぎる:

- 静か(な) → 静かすぎる — too quiet
- 便利(な) → 便利すぎる — too convenient

Irregular: いい → よすぎる (not いすぎる).

The result conjugates as a る-verb from there: すぎる/すぎない/すぎた/すぎました.

## Core use — excess, usually with a negative connotation
Almost always implies "more than is good/appropriate," even when the underlying thing is positive:

- 昨日、食べすぎました。— [I] ate too much yesterday. (mild regret)
- これ、高すぎる! — This is way too expensive!
- 頑張りすぎないでください。— Please don't overdo it [with effort]. (see [[2-requests]] for the ないでください pattern)

## Combining with other patterns
すぎる pairs naturally with the casual regret contraction ちゃう (see [[4-ちゃう]]) and with んです (see [[1-んです]]) when explaining why something's a problem:

- 食べすぎちゃった。— [I] ended up eating too much (oops).
- ちょっと働きすぎなんです。— [The thing is,] [I]'m working a bit too much.

## Notes
- すぎる can be nominalized with 食べ過ぎ (as a noun: "overeating") — common in health/lifestyle contexts: 食べ過ぎは体に悪い。— Overeating is bad for [your] body.
- Distinct from とても/すごく ("very") — すぎる specifically frames something as *excessive/undesirable*, not just intense. とても高い (very expensive, neutral intensity) vs 高すぎる (too expensive, implying it's a problem).

title: ほうがいい - "should" / "better to"
content:
# ほうがいい - "should" / "better to"

The standard way to give advice or state a preference between options — "[you] should do X" / "it's better to do X." One of the most commonly used advice-giving patterns in daily conversation.

## Forming it — affirmative advice
Plain past (た-form, see [[2-て-form]] in 2-verb) + ほうがいい, even though the meaning is about future/hypothetical action, not something already done:

- 早く寝たほうがいいよ。— [You] should sleep early. (lit. "the having-slept-early option is better")
- 病院に行ったほうがいいですよ。— [You] should go to the hospital.
- もっと勉強したほうがいい。— [You] should study more.

Using た-form here (not plain non-past 寝るほうがいい) is the standard, most natural pattern for advice about a specific, immediate situation — using plain non-past instead sounds more like a general statement of preference than concrete advice.

## Forming it — negative advice ("shouldn't")
Plain negative (ない-form, see [[3-plain-vs-polite-form]]) + ほうがいい — note: **not** た-form here, unlike the affirmative:

- お酒を飲まないほうがいいですよ。— [You] shouldn't drink alcohol.
- 無理しないほうがいい。— [You] shouldn't push [yourself] too hard.
- 心配しないほうがいいよ。— [You] shouldn't worry.

This affirmative-uses-た / negative-uses-ない asymmetry is the one thing worth memorizing carefully — mixing them up (using た-form for negative advice) is a common mistake.

## General preference (comparing two options)
Beyond advice to someone, ほうがいい also states a plain preference between two things, tying back to より (see [[3-comparison]] in 3-adjective):

- コーヒーよりお茶のほうがいい。— Tea is better than coffee. (preference, not advice)
- 静かなほうがいいです。— [I] prefer [it] quiet. (な-adjective + な + ほうがいい)

## Softening the directness
ほうがいい can sound quite direct/opinionated on its own — よ or と思う often soften it into a suggestion rather than a command:

- 早く寝たほうがいいと思う。— I think [you] should sleep early. (softer, framed as opinion — see [[../1-particle/5a-と]] for と思う)
- 行ったほうがいいんじゃない? — Isn't it better to go? (very casual, softened via a rhetorical question — see [[1-んです]] for the んじゃない construction)

## Notes
- ほうがいい compares an implied alternative — even without stating it, 早く寝たほうがいい implies "...rather than staying up."
- Don't confuse this ほう (方, "direction/option/side") with 方 as in やり方 ("way of doing") — related etymologically but functioning differently; here ほう always pairs with が+いい to form the comparison structure.

title: かも(しれない) - "might / maybe"
content:
# かも(しれない) - "might / maybe"

Hedges a statement as a possibility, not a certainty — "might be," "maybe," "could be." One of the most common ways to soften a claim in daily casual speech.

## Forming it
Attaches after the plain form of verbs/adjectives, or directly after nouns/な-adjective stems (no だ needed) — full form is かもしれない (casual) / かもしれません (polite), often just clipped to かも in speech:

- 行けないかも(しれない)。— [I] might not be able to go.
- 雨が降るかもしれません。— It might rain.
- 明日は休みかも。— [It] might be a day off tomorrow.
- 高いかもしれない。— [It] might be expensive.

## Bare かも — the natural casual clip
In relaxed daily speech, しれない is very often dropped entirely, leaving just かも as a complete, natural sentence-ender:

- A: 明日来る? — Are you coming tomorrow?
- B: かも。— Maybe. (perfectly complete on its own)
- 忘れちゃったかも。— [I] might have forgotten [it]. (see [[4-ちゃう]] for the ちゃう contraction)

## かも vs かな — different kind of uncertainty
Easy to conflate since both hedge, but they point in different directions: かも estimates the *likelihood of a fact* ("it might be true that..."); かな expresses the speaker's own *wondering/musing* ("I wonder..."), often about their own feelings, plans, or something with no clear answer to look up. See [[9-かな]] for the full comparison.

- 雨が降るかも。— It might rain. (assessing an external fact/probability)
- 雨、降るかな。— I wonder if it'll rain. (musing aloud, less committed to an actual probability estimate)

## Notes
- かも is safe in both casual and polite registers (かもしれません for polite, かも/かもしれない for casual) — unlike some fillers, it scales cleanly across formality.
- Stacks naturally with んです/けど for softening explanations: 遅れるかもしれないんですが。— [I] might be late, so...

title: かな - "I wonder" (self-directed musing)
content:
# かな - "I wonder" (self-directed musing)

Marks a thought as uncertain, musing, or half-directed at yourself rather than a real question posed to the listener — "I wonder...", "maybe I should...", "is it...?" said mostly to think out loud. See [[8-かも]] for how this differs from かも's probability-hedge role.

## Forming it
Attaches after plain form (verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjective/noun without だ):

- 大丈夫かな。— I wonder if [it]'s okay. / Is it okay, I wonder.
- 明日、晴れるかな。— I wonder if [it]'ll be sunny tomorrow.
- 何時かな。— I wonder what time it is.
- 行こうかな。— Maybe I'll go. (volitional + かな — see [[../2-verb/7-volitional-form]] — softens a decision into a half-formed intention)

## Musing vs. asking — the key distinction
Unlike a real question (〜ですか), かな doesn't strongly demand an answer — it's often said with no listener at all, or said near someone as a soft, low-pressure way of thinking aloud that they *could* respond to but aren't obligated to:

- どうしようかな。— What should [I] do, I wonder. (genuinely undecided, thinking out loud)
- これでいいかな? — Is this okay, I wonder? (softer than これでいいですか — inviting a casual opinion rather than formally asking)

This is why かな shows up constantly in inner monologue, diary writing, and low-key conversational asides — it's the sound of someone actively deciding or checking their own uncertainty in real time.

## かな + negative — hoping/wondering about something not happening
かな pairs with negative form to wonder whether something *won't* happen, often carrying a hopeful undertone:

- 雨、降らないかな。— I hope it doesn't rain. (lit. "I wonder if it won't rain" — reads as a soft wish)
- 誰か来ないかな。— I wonder if someone will come. (hoping someone shows up)

## A note on real-world usage: code-switching into English speech
かな shows up often even when Japanese speakers are otherwise speaking English — especially in mixed-language workplace conversation (e.g. bilingual teams, like at Rakuten). It gets dropped in at the end of an English sentence or as a standalone murmur, because it captures a "musing/half-committed" tone that English doesn't have a single clean equivalent for ("I think so, kana" / "maybe... kana" / just a trailing "...kana~"). Hearing it mixed into English isn't broken grammar — it's a deliberate borrow of the nuance, same function as in pure Japanese: signaling "I'm still deciding/not fully sure," said as much to themselves as to you. Worth recognizing as a genuine, common code-switch rather than an error or quirk specific to one speaker.

## Notes
- かな can double up for extra hesitation: かなあ (drawn out) — even softer, more drawn-out uncertainty.
