- Don't confuse か+な (this pattern) with な as the casual masculine command-negation particle (行くな — don't go) — unrelated, context (preceding plain form + full sentence intonation) makes it obvious which is meant.

title: だろう / でしょう(でしょ) - "probably" / confirmation tag
content:
# だろう / でしょう(でしょ) - "probably" / confirmation tag

Expresses a confident guess ("probably X") or seeks/asserts agreement with a rising tone ("...right?"). だろう is the plain-form register, でしょう the polite — でしょ is でしょう's casual clip, extremely common as a tag question.

## Forming it
Attaches after plain form (dropping だ for nouns/な-adjectives):

- 明日は晴れるだろう。— [It]'ll probably be sunny tomorrow. (plain, more common in narration/writing or masculine-leaning casual speech)
- 明日は晴れるでしょう。— [It]'ll probably be sunny tomorrow. (polite, common in weather forecasts, formal predictions)
- 彼はもう帰っただろう。— He's probably already gone home.
- 学生だろう。/ 学生でしょう。— [They]'re probably a student.

## "Probably" — confident prediction
The core use: stating a likely outcome with more confidence than かも (see [[8-かも]]), but still short of certainty:

- 田中さんは来るでしょう。— Tanaka will probably come.
- 高いだろうと思う。— I think [it]'s probably expensive. (stacks with と思う, see [[../1-particle/5a-と]])

Compare the confidence ladder: かも (might, genuinely uncertain) < かな (wondering, undecided) < だろう/でしょう (probably, fairly confident) < plain assertion (certain).

## でしょ — casual confirmation tag ("...right?")
Clipped でしょ, said with rising intonation, asks the listener to confirm or agree — similar territory to ね (see [[../1-particle/6a-ね]]), but でしょ carries more of "I'm pretty confident I'm right, back me up" rather than ね's neutral "don't you agree too":

- すごいでしょ! — Pretty amazing, right?! (showing off, expecting agreement)
- おいしいでしょ? — Tasty, right? (confident it's true, checking the listener agrees)
- だから言ったでしょ! — [That's why] I told you [so], right?! (mildly scolding — "I was right")

## でしょ vs ね — nuance difference
ね genuinely invites the listener's independent reaction/agreement ("isn't it?" — open to their own take). でしょ leans toward "I already know I'm right, confirm it" — more assertive, sometimes a little smug or playful depending on tone:

- いい天気ですね。— Nice weather, isn't it. (neutral, sharing the observation)
- いい天気でしょ? — Nice weather, right? (implying "I told you it would be" or "see, I was right")

## Notes
- だろう can sound blunt/masculine in casual speech if used carelessly — でしょ is the safer, more universally natural casual choice for the "probably/right?" role in everyday conversation.
- でしょうか is the formal, softened question form ("I wonder if... / would it be...") — distinct from casual でしょ, see the brief mention in [[../1-particle/7-か]].

title: んじゃない(?) - rhetorical "isn't it?" tag
content:
# んじゃない(?) - rhetorical "isn't it?" tag

Floats an opinion or observation as a soft rhetorical question rather than a flat statement — "isn't it...?", "I think it's..., no?" Built from の/ん (see [[../1-particle/4-の]]) + じゃない (casual negative copula, see [[../2-verb/3-plain-vs-polite-form]]), but the negative here isn't literal — it's a rhetorical-question shape, not an actual negation.

## Forming it
Plain form + んじゃない (casual) / んじゃないですか (polite):

- それ、いいんじゃない? — Isn't that good? / I think that's good, no?
- 高いんじゃない? — Isn't [that] expensive?
- 行ったほうがいいんじゃない? — Isn't it better to go? (stacks with ほうがいい, see [[7-ほうがいい]])
- 大丈夫なんじゃないですか。— Isn't [it] probably fine? (polite version, な inserted for na-adjectives/nouns before ん, same as んです — see [[1-んです]])

## Not a real negative — a softened assertion
The literal grammar reads as "isn't it not X" (double negative-shaped), but the actual meaning is a gently floated positive opinion — the rhetorical question shape exists specifically to avoid stating something too bluntly:

- それ、変じゃない? — Isn't that weird? (= I think that's weird, but framed as a question so it's less confrontational)
- できるんじゃない? — Can't [you] probably do it? (= I think you can, encouraging)

## んじゃない vs でしょ vs ね — three ways to float an opinion softly
All three invite some kind of listener reaction, but with different flavors:

| Form | Flavor |
|---|---|
| 〜んじゃない? | "I think X, but I'm floating it as a question" — genuinely open to pushback |
| 〜でしょ? | "I'm confident X is right, confirm it" — see [[10-だろう-でしょう]] |
| 〜ね | "I assume you agree, sharing the feeling" — see [[../1-particle/6a-ね]] |

んじゃない is the most tentative/hedge-y of the three — it's specifically useful when suggesting something without wanting to sound like you're asserting a fact.

## Common daily uses: suggestions and gentle pushback
- 今日は疲れてるし、休んだほうがいいんじゃない? — [You]'re tired today, maybe [you] should rest? (a suggestion, softened)
- それ、違うんじゃない? — Isn't that wrong? / I don't think that's right. (gentle correction, less blunt than 違うよ)

## Notes
- Intonation matters — rising, soft intonation reads as genuinely open/gentle; flatter delivery can sound more like a mild assertion of disagreement, closer to "that's not right, is it."
- んじゃないかな combines this with かな (see [[9-かな]]) for maximum softness/hedging: 大丈夫なんじゃないかな。— I think it's probably okay, though [I'm not totally sure].

title: たことがある - "have done X before" (experience)
content:
# たことがある - "have done X before" (experience)

States that you have experience doing something at some point in the (usually unspecified) past — "I've done X before," "I have experience with X." Extremely common in daily conversation about travel, food, hobbies, and general life experience.

## Forming it
Plain past (た-form, see [[../2-verb/2-て-form]]) + ことがある:

- 日本に行ったことがあります。— [I]'ve been to Japan [before].
- 納豆を食べたことがある。— [I]'ve eaten natto before.
- 富士山に登ったことがありますか。— Have [you] ever climbed Mt. Fuji?

Negative — "never done X":
- 海外に行ったことがない。— [I]'ve never been abroad.
- そんなの聞いたことがありません。— [I]'ve never heard of such a thing.

## Emphasis on experience, not recency or a specific time
This pattern is specifically about the *fact of having done something at least once*, without pinning down when — contrast with plain past, which reports a specific event:

- 日本に行きました。— [I] went to Japan. (a specific, completed trip — implies a known "when")
- 日本に行ったことがあります。— [I]'ve been to Japan [at some point]. (experience/résumé fact, timing irrelevant)

Don't use this pattern for something that just happened or has an obvious specific timeframe — たことがある sounds odd for very recent/specific events (誰かと今日話したことがある sounds strange; just 今日話しました is natural).

## Asking about experience — common conversation starter
〜たことがありますか is one of the most natural ways to make small talk about travel, food, or hobbies:

- 韓国に行ったことがありますか。— Have [you] ever been to Korea?
- この映画、見たことある? — Have [you] seen this movie [before]? (casual, ある without ですか)

## Casual clipping
In relaxed speech, ことがある often drops the が: ことある — very common, natural contraction:

- それ、聞いたことある。— [I]'ve heard of that.
- やったことない。— [I]'ve never done [it].

## Notes
- Not to be confused with things happening habitually (that's ている/たり〜たりする, see [[../2-verb/10-たり]]) — たことがある is strictly about whether an experience exists at all in your history, once or more, not how often.
- こと here nominalizes the verb (turning "did X" into "the experience of having done X") — the same こと used in 〜ことができる (potential, see [[../2-verb/5-potential-form]]).

title: Verb-ない? - casual invitation
content:
# Verb-ない? - casual invitation

A plain negative question used specifically to invite someone to do something together — "wanna...?", "won't you...?" One of the most natural, common ways to propose plans casually, distinct from んじゃない's rhetorical-opinion use (see [[11-んじゃない]]).

## Forming it
Plain negative (see [[../2-verb/3-plain-vs-polite-form]]) + rising intonation, written with a question mark in casual text:

- 一緒に行かない? — Wanna go together?
- お茶しない? — Wanna grab tea?
- 今度、映画見ない? — Wanna watch a movie sometime?
- 週末、遊ばない? — Wanna hang out this weekend?

## Why negative form for a positive invitation
The negative framing ("won't you do X?") softens the invitation compared to a flat positive suggestion — it leaves room for the other person to say no without it feeling like they're rejecting a direct proposal. This mirrors ませんか as its polite counterpart (see the note in [[../2-verb/7-volitional-form]]):

- 行かない? — Wanna go? (casual, plain negative)
- 行きませんか。— Won't [you] go [with me]? (polite negative — same softening logic, formal register)

Both are gentler than a bare volitional 行こう (let's go — see [[../2-verb/7-volitional-form]]), which reads more like a decision already being made rather than an open invitation.

## Responding to an invitation
Natural casual responses:

- いいね、行こう! — Sounds good, let's go! (accepting, switching to volitional)
- うん、いいよ。— Yeah, sure.
- ごめん、今日はちょっと... — Sorry, today's a bit... (declining, trailing off — see [[../5-filler/5-ちょっと]] for this soft-refusal pattern)

## Distinguishing from a real negative question
Context and intonation separate this from an actual "aren't you doing X?" question — an invitation-ない? is warm/forward-looking (proposing something new), while a literal negative question usually checks on an existing plan or fact:

- 行かない? — Wanna go? (proposing something new)
- 行かないの? — [You]'re not going? (checking on an already-known plan, mild surprise — see the の nuance in [[../1-particle/4-の]])

## Notes
- This pattern works with any verb, not just social activities — 食べない? (want to eat [some]?), 座らない? (wanna sit?) — anywhere you'd propose a shared action.
- Purely casual register — for anyone you'd need politeness with, use ませんか instead.

title: てほしい - "want someone [else] to do X"
content:
# てほしい - "want someone [else] to do X"

Expresses wanting another person to do something — the other-directed counterpart to たい (see [[../2-verb/4-たい-form]]), which is strictly about the speaker's own desire to act.

## Forming it
て-form (see [[../2-verb/2-て-form]]) + ほしい, which conjugates as a regular い-adjective:

- 来てほしい。— [I] want [you] to come.
- 手伝ってほしいんですが。— [I]'d like [you] to help, if [you] could. (stacking with んです, see [[1-んです]], for a softer request-flavored statement)
- もっと話してほしかった。— [I] wish [he]'d talked more. (past: てほしかった)

Negative — wanting someone *not* to do something:
- 心配してほしくない。— [I] don't want [you] to worry.
- もう来てほしくない。— [I] don't want [you] to come anymore.

## たい vs てほしい — who's doing the action
This is the one thing to keep straight: たい attaches when the *speaker* is the one who wants to act; てほしい attaches when the speaker wants *someone else* to act:

- 行きたい。— [I] want to go. (I'm the one going)
- 行ってほしい。— [I] want [you] to go. (someone else is going, I want it to happen)

Mixing these up is a common learner slip, since English "want" doesn't grammaticalize this distinction the same way.

## てほしい vs a direct request (てください)
てほしい states a desire/wish about someone else's action — it's more of an expressed hope than an actual command, and often softer/more indirect than directly asking with てください (see [[2-requests]]):

- 手伝ってください。— Please help [me]. (direct request)
- 手伝ってほしいな。— [I] wish [you'd] help [me]. (expressing a wish, softer, sometimes used when not directly asking, just voicing a hope)

てほしい is common when talking *about* wanting something from someone who isn't present, or when softening a wish rather than issuing an instruction.

## Notes
- Like たい, てほしい directly describes the speaker's own feeling — for describing a third party's wish about someone else, hedge with と思っている or がっている constructions (long-tail, not needed early — see the third-person note in [[../2-verb/4-たい-form]] for the parallel logic with たい).
- Often paired with な/よね for a musing, wishful tone in casual speech: 早く終わってほしいな。— [I] wish it would end soon.

title: なんか - filler / "like" / "something"
content:
# なんか - filler / "like" / "something"

One of the most common words in casual spoken Japanese, doing three related jobs: a thinking filler, a casual "something," and a non-exhaustive example marker. If you listen to any natural conversation, なんか shows up constantly.

## Pure filler ("like," "um," "sort of")
Dropped in at the start of a sentence or mid-thought while organizing what to say, or to soften a statement — functionally close to English "like" as a filler:

- なんか、疲れた。— Like, [I'm] tired. / Somehow [I'm] tired.
- なんか、今日変な日だった。— Today was, like, a weird day.
- それ、なんか違うと思う。— I think that's, like, not quite right.

This use carries no fixed literal meaning — it's a hedge/pause word, similar to how "like" or "kind of" gets inserted in casual English speech. Overusing it is a real tic (native speakers do it too, in bursts), but as a learner it's more important to *recognize* it than to force it into your own speech constantly.

## Casual contraction of 何か ("something")
なんか is the everyday spoken contraction of 何か (see the indefinite-pronoun note in [[7-か]]):

- なんか食べたい。— [I] want to eat something.
- なんか変な音がした。— [I] heard some kind of weird sound.
- なんか用? — [You] need something [from me]? / What's up? (casual, slightly blunt)

Compare with the filler use: 何か食べたい (want to eat *something*, specific unspecified object) vs なんか、食べたい (like, [I] want to eat — filler softening the whole sentence, no specific "something" implied). Context and what follows なんか usually disambiguates.

## Non-exhaustive example marker ("things like X")
Attaches after a noun to suggest it as one example among similar things — overlaps with とか (see [[13-とか]]) but slightly more casual/dismissive in tone, sometimes implying mild distance or a lack of enthusiasm:

- コーヒーなんか好きです。— [I] like things like coffee. (coffee as one example of what I like)
- 一人でなんか行けないよ。— [I] can't go alone or anything [like that]. (なんか reinforcing "there's no way")

## Vague dissatisfaction / "something's off" feeling
なんか often precedes a vague, hard-to-pin-down feeling or impression — "somehow," "for some reason":

- なんか変。— Something's weird [about this]. (can't quite say what)
- なんか嫌だ。— [I] just don't like it, somehow. (no clear reason given)

## Notes
- なんか is almost exclusively spoken/casual — avoid it in polite or written contexts; そうですね-style fillers or a clean sentence without it are better there.
- Don't confuse なんか (filler/something/example-marker, this file) with なにか, its full, unabbreviated written form — they're the same word, なんか is just the natural spoken contraction.

title: あの / あのー - hesitation / attention-getter
content:
# あの / あのー - hesitation / attention-getter

Opens a sentence to get someone's attention, hesitate before saying something (often awkward or a request), or politely interrupt. One of the most reflexive fillers in Japanese — often the very first sound out of someone's mouth when approaching a stranger.

## Getting someone's attention / approaching a stranger
The standard, polite way to open an interaction with someone you don't know — a waiter, a stranger on the street, a store clerk:

- あの、すみません。— Um, excuse me.
- あのー、これはいくらですか。— Um, how much is this?

Functionally similar to "excuse me" or "um" in English as a conversation-opener, not a request itself — it just signals "I'm about to say something to you."

## Hesitation before a request or awkward topic
あの (often lengthened to あのー while thinking) buys a beat before saying something potentially uncomfortable, asking a favor, or bringing up a sensitive topic:

- あの、ちょっとお願いがあるんですが。— Um, [I] have a bit of a favor to ask...
- あのー、実は... — Um, actually...

Pairs naturally with the softening んですが/んですけど pattern (see [[1-んです]] in 4-pattern and [[12-けど]] in 1-particle).

## Length signals hesitation level
A short あの is a quick attention-getter; a drawn-out あのー signals more hesitation or that the speaker is actively formulating what to say next — similar to how "um..." can be short or stretched out in English depending on how much someone is stalling.

## Notes
- あの is polite/neutral register — safe with strangers, service staff, and in formal contexts, unlike more casual fillers like なんか (see [[1-なんか]]).
- Don't confuse this あの with あの as a demonstrative adjective ("that ~ over there," as in あの人 — that person) — same word, different job; context (start of a sentence with nothing following directly = filler; あの + noun = demonstrative) makes it clear.

title: えっと / えーと - thinking filler
content:
# えっと / えーと - thinking filler

Pure "let me think" filler — used while recalling information, deciding what to say, or working something out in real time. Unlike あの (see [[2-あの]]), which opens an interaction, えっと is used mid-thought, often when put on the spot.

## Buying time to think
Dropped in right before or during the moment of trying to remember or calculate something:

- えっと、明日は... 火曜日だ。— Um, tomorrow is... [it]'s Tuesday.
- えっと、名前なんだっけ。— Uh, what was [their] name again...
- えーと、どこまで話したっけ。— Um, where was I in the story...

## Answering a question you need a second to think about
Extremely common right after being asked something that requires a moment of recall or calculation:

- Q: 全部でいくらですか。— How much is it in total?
- A: えっと... 3000円です。— Um... it's 3000 yen.

## えっと vs あの — different jobs
えっと is about the speaker's own thinking process (internal, "let me recall/figure this out"); あの is about addressing the listener (external, "hey, before I say this..."). They can even stack: あの、えっと... — Um, uh... (hesitating both to speak up and to figure out what to say).

## Notes
- えっと/えーと is neutral register — fine in both casual and polite conversation, since it's just a natural pause, not a stylistic choice like なんか (see [[1-なんか]]).
- Lengthening the ー (えーーーと) mirrors dragging out "uhhhh" in English — more stalling, same function.

title: やっぱり / やっぱ - "as I thought" / "after all"
content:
# やっぱり / やっぱ - "as I thought" / "after all"

Signals that a conclusion matches what you suspected, or marks a change of mind back to an earlier instinct. One of the most frequently used words in casual Japanese conversation — やっぱ is the even more casual, clipped version.

## Confirming a hunch ("as I thought" / "I knew it")
Used when reality confirms what you already suspected or predicted:

- やっぱり雨が降った。— [It] rained after all, [just as I thought].
- やっぱり彼は来なかった。— [As expected], he didn't come.
- やっぱりそうだと思った! — I knew it! (lit. "I thought it was as I expected, after all")

## Reverting to an earlier choice ("after all," "on second thought")
Marks changing your mind back toward something you'd considered before, or reconsidering a decision mid-stream:

- やっぱりコーヒーにする。— [I]'ll have coffee after all. (changed mind, back to original instinct)
- やっぱりやめよう。— Let's not, after all. / On second thought, let's not.
- 行くか迷ったけど、やっぱり行くことにした。— [I] was torn about going, but decided to go after all.

This "changing your mind, landing back on your gut instinct" use is extremely common in daily decision-making speech — ordering food, making plans, etc.

## Standalone reaction
やっぱり! by itself is a common one-word reaction meaning "I knew it!" / "just as expected" — reacting to news that confirms a suspicion.

## やっぱ — casual clip
やっぱ is just やっぱり with the last syllable dropped, used identically but sounds more casual/quick — common in relaxed spoken Japanese:

- やっぱ無理。— Nah, can't do it after all.

## Notes
- やっぱり doesn't attach grammatically to anything — it's a standalone adverb that sits at the start of (or floats within) a sentence, unlike particles that attach directly to words.
- Distinct from もう一度 (once more) or また (again) — やっぱり is specifically about matching an expectation or reverting to an earlier inclination, not repetition.

title: ちょっと - "a little" / softening hedge
content:
# ちょっと - "a little" / softening hedge

Literally "a little/a bit," but its real daily job is softening requests, refusals, and criticism — one of the most reflexively used words in polite/casual Japanese to avoid sounding blunt.

## Literal "a little"
The base meaning, quantifying something as small in degree or amount:

- ちょっと待ってください。— Please wait a moment.
- ちょっと高いですね。— [It]'s a bit expensive, isn't it.
- ちょっとだけ食べた。— [I] ate just a little. (see [[9a-だけ]] in 1-particle for the stacking with だけ)

## Softening a refusal ("that's a bit...")
ちょっと is the go-to way to decline or express reluctance without directly saying no — trailing off is completely normal and understood as a soft "no":

- 今日はちょっと... — Today's a bit... [not good for me]. (trails off, understood as declining)
- それはちょっと難しいです。— That's a bit difficult. (softer than 無理です/できません — "impossible/can't do it")

Leaving the sentence unfinished after ちょっと is not rude or incomplete — it's the expected, polite way to say no in many daily situations, especially declining invitations. See [[../8-conjunction/2-trailing-off]] for this same trailing-off habit across けど/し/から/て-form.

## Softening a request or interruption
Similar to あの (see [[2-あの]]), ちょっと often opens a request to make it feel smaller/less imposing:

- ちょっと聞いてもいいですか。— Can I ask [you] something [real quick]?
- ちょっとすみません。— Excuse me a moment. (getting past someone, interrupting briefly)

## Softening criticism or a negative observation
Cushions a critical or negative statement so it lands less harshly:

- それはちょっと... — That's a bit [off/not great]. (implied criticism, unfinished)
- ちょっとうるさいよ。— [That]'s a little loud, y'know. (softer than 直接 うるさい! alone)

## Notes
- ちょっと is safe across both polite and casual registers — one of the most universally usable softeners in the language, unlike casual-only fillers such as なんか (see [[1-なんか]] in 5-filler).
- ちょっと + trailing silence (no verb after) is a distinct, very common pattern worth specifically getting comfortable with — it's not a sentence fragment mistake, it's how native speakers decline things gracefully.

title: まあ - "well" / hedging filler
content:
# まあ - "well" / hedging filler

A soft hedge meaning roughly "well," "I guess," "more or less" — downplays certainty, tones down a statement, or signals reluctant acceptance.

## Downplaying / "I guess" / "more or less"
Softens a statement so it doesn't sound too definite or strong:

- まあ、いいか。— Well, [it]'s fine [I guess]. / Oh well, whatever.
- まあ、そうですね。— Well, I suppose so. (agreeing, but without full conviction)
- まあまあです。— [It]'s so-so / okay, I guess. (doubled まあまあ specifically means "mediocre/average")

## Reluctant acceptance / settling for something
Signals accepting a situation without being fully enthusiastic about it:

- まあ、仕方ないね。— Well, [it] can't be helped, I guess.
- まあ、いいんじゃない? — Well, [I guess it]'s fine? (mild, unenthusiastic approval)

## Softening before disagreeing or qualifying
Often opens a sentence right before a mild pushback or qualification, cushioning it:

- まあ、それはそうだけど... — Well, that's true, but... (see [[../1-particle/12-けど]] for the けど half of this pairing)

## まあまあ — "so-so" (distinct doubled form)
Worth knowing as its own fixed phrase — answering "how was it?" with まあまあ means "eh, okay/average," neither good nor bad:

- Q: 映画どうだった? — How was the movie?
- A: まあまあだった。— It was so-so.

## Notes
- まあ is safe in both casual and moderately polite speech — less blunt/casual-only than なんか (see [[1-なんか]]), closer in register to ちょっと (see [[5-ちょっと]]).
- Don't confuse the filler まあ with 前 (まえ, "before/front") — unrelated words, distinguishable by context and that まあ never takes に/の the way 前 does.

title: というか - "or rather" / self-correction filler
content:
# というか - "or rather" / self-correction filler

Used to rephrase, correct, or refine what you just said (or are about to say) mid-sentence — "or rather," "I mean," "more like." Literally "or [if I were to] say" (と + 言う + か, see [[../1-particle/5a-と]] for と's quoting function).

## Rephrasing / correcting yourself mid-thought
Signals swapping out a word or framing for a more accurate one, right after saying it:

- 楽しい、というか、面白かった。— [It] was fun — or rather, interesting. (refining the word choice)
- 忙しい、というか、時間がない。— [I]'m busy — I mean, [I] don't have time. (clarifying what "busy" actually means here)

## Pushing back on a premise gently
というか can also redirect a conversation, gently suggesting the other person's framing is slightly off before offering a better one:

- A: それ、難しいね。— That's hard, huh.
- B: というか、無理じゃない? — I mean, isn't it [just] impossible? (reframing "hard" as "impossible")

## Opening with a correction to what was just implied
Common right at the start of a response, right after hearing something you want to gently push back on or reframe:

- というか、それ聞いてないんだけど。— Wait, I mean, [I] wasn't told that. (mild pushback, softened by というか instead of a blunt correction)

## というか vs まあ — different jobs
まあ (see [[6-まあ]]) hedges/downplays; というか actively rephrases or corrects. They can even combine: まあ、というか... — Well, I mean...

## Notes
- というか is casual-to-neutral register — fine in relaxed conversation, less at home in formal/polite contexts where a fuller rephrase (それより, むしろ) would be more appropriate.
- Functions similarly to inserting "I mean" or "or rather" mid-sentence in English — a live self-edit, not a planned part of the sentence structure.

title: じゃあ / じゃ - "well then" / "so" transition
content:
# じゃあ / じゃ - "well then" / "so" transition

Opens a response or shifts into an action/decision based on what was just said — "well then," "so," "in that case." One of the most common ways to transition a conversation forward in daily Japanese.

## Reacting to information — "well then" / "in that case"
Signals that what follows is a natural conclusion or reaction to what the other person just said:

- A: 今日は雨みたいだよ。— Looks like rain today. B: じゃあ、傘を持っていこう。— Well then, [I]'ll bring an umbrella. (see [[../4-pattern/5-appearance-hearsay]] for みたい)
- A: もう時間だよ。— It's already time. B: じゃあ、行くね。— Okay then, [I]'m off.

## Transitioning into an action or closing
Extremely common to open the final line of an exchange — wrapping up and moving into what happens next:

- じゃあ、始めましょうか。— Well then, shall [we] begin? (see [[../2-verb/7-volitional-form]] for ましょうか)
- じゃあね! — See ya! / Bye then! (a very common casual goodbye)
- じゃあ、また明日。— Okay, see [you] tomorrow then.

## じゃ — casual clip
じゃ is じゃあ shortened further, used identically but slightly more clipped/quick, common in fast casual speech:

- じゃ、行こうか。— Well, shall we go?

## じゃあ vs では — formality register
では is the more formal/written equivalent of じゃあ, appearing in business speech, presentations, and writing (では、始めます — well then, let's begin) — じゃあ/じゃ is what you'll hear in casual daily conversation almost exclusively.

## Notes
- じゃあ is unrelated to じゃない (casual negative copula, see [[../2-verb/3-plain-vs-polite-form]]) despite the visual similarity — じゃあ is a standalone transition word, じゃない is a conjugated negative form attached to something.
- Often paired with a beat of thought before it, functioning like えっと (see [[3-えっと]]) crossed with a decision — じゃあ often marks the moment a decision gets made, not just idle transition.

title: Counters (助数詞) — how to count things
content:
# Counters (助数詞) — how to count things

Japanese doesn't count "two books" the way English does — every noun category has its own counter suffix attached to a number, and the numbers themselves sometimes shift sound depending on which counter follows. Survival-critical: ordering food, buying things, giving your age, telling time, counting people, all route through this system.

## Two number systems
Japanese has native Japanese numbers (used for a small, closed set of generic counting) and Sino-Japanese numbers (used with virtually all counters):

**Native (native Japanese, only goes 1–10, then switches to Sino-Japanese):**
ひとつ、ふたつ、みっつ、よっつ、いつつ、むっつ、ななつ、やっつ、ここのつ、とお

Used generically for objects with no specific counter, or when you don't know/remember the right counter — a safe fallback: りんごを 3つ ください。— [Give me] 3 apples, please. (using つ instead of 個)

**Sino-Japanese (the base system nearly all counters attach to):**
いち、に、さん、よん(し)、ご、ろく、なな(しち)、はち、きゅう(く)、じゅう

4, 7, and 9 each have two readings (よん/し, なな/しち, きゅう/く) — which one is used depends on the specific counter or context; both exist because し and しち sound too similar and get avoided in speech, and し/く carry unlucky death/suffering associations avoided in certain contexts (hospitals, gift quantities).

## Common counters

| Counter | Used for | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 人 (にん/り) | people | 一人 (ひとり), 二人 (ふたり), 三人 (さんにん) — irregular for 1 and 2! |
| つ | generic objects (native numbers) | 一つ、二つ、三つ |
| 個 (こ) | small general objects | 一個、二個、三個 |
| 枚 (まい) | flat things (paper, tickets, plates) | 一枚、二枚 |
| 本 (ほん/ぼん/ぽん) | long cylindrical things (bottles, pens, trains) | 一本 (いっぽん), 二本 (にほん), 三本 (さんぼん) |
| 冊 (さつ) | bound things (books, magazines) | 一冊、二冊 |
| 匹 (ひき/びき/ぴき) | small animals (cats, dogs, bugs) | 一匹 (いっぴき), 二匹 (にひき) |
| 頭 (とう) | large animals (cows, elephants) | 一頭、二頭 |
| 台 (だい) | machines, vehicles | 一台、二台 |
| 階 (かい/がい) | floors of a building | 一階 (いっかい), 二階 (にかい) |
| 歳/才 (さい) | age | 一歳、二十歳 (はたち — irregular!) |
| 円 (えん) | yen | 百円、千円 |
| 時 (じ) | hour (clock time) | 一時、二時、四時 (よじ, not よんじ) |
| 分 (ふん/ぷん) | minutes | 一分 (いっぷん), 二分 (にふん), 三分 (さんぷん) |

## The sound-shift trap
Certain counters starting with は/ひ/ふ (本、匹、分, etc.) trigger consonant shifts on 1, 3, 6, 8, and 10 — this is genuinely irregular and just needs memorizing per counter, following patterns like:

- 一 + 本/匹/分/階 → いっぽん/いっぴき/いっぷん/いっかい (っ + p-sound)
- 三 + 本 → さんぼん (b-sound, not h)
- 六/八/十 + 本 → ろっぽん/はっぽん/じゅっぽん (っ + p-sound again)

There's no universal shortcut — but the pattern of "1, 3, 6, 8, 10 are the troublemakers with は-row counters" is worth knowing so you're not caught off guard.

## 人 — the irregular counter for people
The most commonly used counter has genuinely irregular readings for 1 and 2, then becomes regular:

- 一人 (ひとり) — one person
- 二人 (ふたり) — two people
- 三人 (さんにん), 四人 (よにん), 五人 (ごにん)... — regular にん from 3 onward

## Asking "how many?"
The question word matches the counting system in use:

- いくつ — how many (with native つ counting, or asking age casually: おいくつですか — how old are you, polite)
- 何 + counter — how many, with Sino-Japanese counters: 何人 (なんにん, how many people), 何個 (なんこ, how many pieces), 何歳 (なんさい, how old)

## Notes
- When unsure of the exact counter for something, つ (native numbers) is a safe generic fallback for physical objects — natives will understand even if it's not the "textbook precise" counter.
- The most natural position for a number+counter is right after the noun's particle, floating before the verb: りんごを3つ買った。— [I] bought 3 apples. Placing it before the noun with の (3つのりんごを買った) is also grammatical and common, just a slightly different emphasis — both are fine to use.

title: こそあど - demonstrative system (this/that/where/how)
content:
# こそあど - demonstrative system (this/that/where/how)

A systematic family of reference words built on four prefixes — こ (near speaker), そ (near listener / already mentioned), あ (far from both / shared knowledge), ど (question) — each combined with the same set of suffixes for "thing," "place," "direction," "kind," and "manner." Learn the pattern once, get the whole system.

## The grid

| | こ (near me) | そ (near you / mentioned) | あ (far from both) | ど (which/where?) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Thing | これ (this) | それ (that) | あれ (that, over there) | どれ (which one) |
| Place | ここ (here) | そこ (there) | あそこ (over there) | どこ (where) |
| Direction | こちら/こっち (this way) | そちら/そっち (that way) | あちら/あっち (that way, far) | どちら/どっち (which way) |
| Kind (+noun) | この (this ~) | その (that ~) | あの (that ~, far) | どの (which ~) |
| Adjectival | こんな (this kind of) | そんな (that kind of) | あんな (that kind of, far) | どんな (what kind of) |
| Manner | こう (like this) | そう (like that) | ああ (like that, far) | どう (how) |

## こ/そ/あ — physical distance vs. conversational distance
Two overlapping systems:

**Physical**: こ = close to the speaker, そ = close to the listener, あ = far from both.
- これ、ください。— This one, please. (near you, the speaker)
- それ、何ですか。— What's that? (near the listener)
- あそこに猫がいる。— There's a cat over there. (far from both)

**Conversational/discourse**: そ = something the listener just mentioned or that's newly introduced into the conversation; あ = something both speaker and listener already know about/share context on (shared memory, not physically present).

- A: 昨日、いい映画を見たよ。— I saw a good movie yesterday. B: それ、何て映画? — What movie [is] that? (そ — referring to what was just said, not physically present)
- あの店、また行きたいね。— [I] want to go to that shop again, huh. (あ — a shared reference both people already know, not currently visible)

## この/その/あの/どの — before a noun (attributive)
These must be directly followed by a noun — they cannot stand alone the way これ/それ/あれ/どれ can:

- この本。— This book. (not ~~これ本~~)
- どの人ですか。— Which person is it?

Note: あの here is the same word as the filler あの (see [[../5-filler/2-あの]]) — genuinely the same demonstrative, just grammaticalized into a filler/attention-getter when used alone at the start of a sentence.

## こんな/そんな/あんな/どんな — describing a kind/type
Function like な-adjectives, describing "this kind of," "that sort of":

- こんな服が好きです。— [I] like this kind of clothes.
- そんなこと言わないで。— Don't say something like that. (see [[2-requests]] for ないで)
- どんな音楽が好きですか。— What kind of music do [you] like?

## こう/そう/ああ/どう — manner ("like this/that/how")
Describe *how* something is done or *how* something is:

- こうしてください。— Please do [it] like this.
- どうしましたか。— What happened? / What's wrong? (extremely common daily question — see the んですか pairing in [[1-んです]]: どうしたんですか)
- そう思います。— I think so. (そう here overlaps with the appearance/hearsay そう — see [[5-appearance-hearsay]])

## Notes
- どう/どんな/どちら are the question-row — they combine with か to form indefinites, mirroring 何か/誰か (see [[../1-particle/7-か]]): どこか (somewhere), どれか (some one of them).
- こちら/そちら/あちら/どちら (formal) vs こっち/そっち/あっち/どっち (casual) — same meaning, different register; the casual っち forms are far more common in daily speech.

title: Question words — 何 / 誰 / いつ / いくら / なぜ・どうして
content:
# Question words — 何 / 誰 / いつ / いくら / なぜ・どうして

The core interrogatives that live outside the こそあど grid (see [[1-こそあど]] for どこ/どれ/どう/どの/どんな, which are part of that system). These are basic, load-bearing daily vocabulary — asking what, who, when, how much, and why.

## 何 (なに/なん) — what
Two readings depending on what follows — なん before certain consonants (especially な/だ/の rows, and counters), なに elsewhere. Both common, no need to overthink which to use in most cases:

- これは何ですか。— What is this? (なん before です)
- 何を食べますか。— What will [you] eat? (なに before を)
- 何時ですか。— What time is it? (なんじ)
- 何色が好きですか。— What color do [you] like? (なにいろ)

何+か/でも/も builds indefinites, already covered from the か side (see [[../1-particle/7-か]]):
- 何か食べたい。— [I] want to eat something.
- 何でもいい。— Anything's fine.
- 何もない。— There's nothing. (with negative verb)

## 誰 (だれ) / どなた — who
だれ is the standard casual/neutral form; どなた is the polite version, used with strangers or in formal contexts:

- 誰ですか。— Who is it?
- あれは誰の傘ですか。— Whose umbrella is that? (誰の — see [[../1-particle/4-の]] for の as possession)
- どなたですか。— Who may I ask is calling/speaking? (polite, e.g. answering the phone)

誰+か/も follows the same indefinite pattern as 何:
- 誰か来た。— Someone came.
- 誰もいない。— There's no one [here]. (with negative)

## いつ — when
Straightforward, no reading variation, works for both specific and general time questions:

- いつ行きますか。— When will [you] go?
- 誕生日はいつですか。— When's [your] birthday?

いつか (someday) and いつも (always) are the indefinite/extended forms, both extremely common:
- いつか日本に行きたい。— [I] want to go to Japan someday.
- 彼はいつも忙しい。— He's always busy.

## いくら — how much (price/cost)
Specifically for money/cost — not to be confused with いくつ (how many, see the counters note in [[../6-counter/1-counters]]):

- これはいくらですか。— How much is this?
- 全部でいくらになりますか。— How much does it come to in total?

## なぜ / どうして — why
Both mean "why," but どうして is the more common, natural everyday choice; なぜ leans more formal/written, or is used when the question carries a heavier, more serious weight:

- どうして遅れたの? — Why were [you] late? (casual, everyday)
- なぜですか。— Why [is that]? (more formal, or asking about something significant)

どうして also works as a genuine "how" in older/formal usage, but in modern daily conversation it's almost always "why" — for "how," see どう / どうやって below.

## どう / どうやって — how
どう (see [[1-こそあど]]'s manner row) asks about a state or opinion ("how is it"); どうやって specifically asks about method ("by what means/how do you do it"):

- 元気? どう? — How's it going? / How are you?
- これ、どうやって作るの? — How do [you] make this?
- 会社までどうやって行きますか。— How do [you] get to the office? (asking about method — train, walk, etc.)

## Quick reference

| Word | Asks about |
|---|---|
| 何 (なに/なん) | what |
| 誰 (だれ) / どなた | who |
| いつ | when |
| いくら | how much (cost) |
| いくつ | how many (see [[../6-counter/1-counters]]) |
| なぜ / どうして | why |
| どう | how (state/opinion) |
| どうやって | how (method) |
| どこ/どれ/どの/どんな | where/which/what kind (see [[1-こそあど]]) |

## Notes
- Question words never take は as their own topic marker in the question itself — they take が when they're the subject (誰が来ましたか, not 誰は), matching the new-information rule for が (see [[../1-particle/1b-が]]).
- Answers to a question-word question typically echo back with が for the same reason: 田中さんが来ました, not 田中さんは来ました, when directly answering 誰が来ましたか.

title: そして / それから / でも - sentence-starting conjunctions
content:
# そして / それから / でも - sentence-starting conjunctions

Connect two separate, complete sentences — distinct from clause-attaching particles like けど (see [[../1-particle/12-けど]]), し (see [[../1-particle/15-し]]), or から (see [[../1-particle/8a-から]]), which all glue onto the end of the *first* clause. These instead stand alone at the start of the *second* sentence, after a full stop.

## そして — "and then" (formal-leaning sequencing)
Connects two sentences in sequence, often with a sense of a notable next step — common in narration, writing, and somewhat formal/deliberate speech:

- 朝ごはんを食べた。そして、仕事に行った。— [I] ate breakfast. And then, [I] went to work.
- 頑張った。そして、成功した。— [I] worked hard. And [then], [I] succeeded.

そして can feel a little formal/narrative for very casual daily chat — in relaxed conversation, that それから below, or just starting the next sentence with nothing at all, is often more natural.

## それから — "after that" / "and then" (casual, everyday sequencing)
The everyday, casual equivalent of そして for listing what happened next, or adding one more item to a list:

- 学校に行った。それから、友達と遊んだ。— [I] went to school. After that, [I] hung out with friends.
- パンを買った。それから、牛乳も買った。— [I] bought bread. And [then I] also bought milk.

それから also works to add an afterthought item to a list, similar to "oh, and also":

- コーヒーをください。それから、水も。— Coffee, please. And also water.

## でも — "but" (standalone, sentence-initial)
The sentence-starting counterpart to clause-attached けど (see [[../1-particle/12-けど]]) — same meaning, different structural slot. でも opens a new sentence that contrasts with the one before it:

- 行きたい。でも、時間がない。— [I] want to go. But, [I] don't have time.
- 高い。でも、買った。— [It]'s expensive. But, [I] bought [it].

Compare directly with けど gluing the same idea into one sentence:
- 行きたいけど、時間がない。— [I] want to go, but [I] don't have time. (one sentence)
- 行きたい。でも、時間がない。— [I] want to go. But [I] don't have time. (two sentences, でも opens the second)

Both are common and largely interchangeable in meaning — the choice is about pacing/emphasis: でも as its own sentence gives the contrast more weight/pause than けど folded into a single breath.

## Quick comparison: clause-attached vs. sentence-starting

| Meaning | Attaches to end of clause | Starts a new sentence |
|---|---|---|
| but | 〜けど (see [[../1-particle/12-けど]]) | でも |
| and then / next | 〜て (see [[../2-verb/2-て-form]]) | そして / それから |
| because... so | 〜から (see [[../1-particle/8a-から]]) | だから (see note below) |

## Notes
- でも here is unrelated to でも as an indefinite-extending suffix (何でも — anything, 誰でも — anyone) — same spelling, different grammatical job; context makes it obvious.
- だから ("so, therefore") is the natural fourth member of this family — the sentence-starting counterpart to から, e.g. 疲れた。だから、休んだ。— [I] was tired. So, [I] rested. Worth its own note if this folder grows further.

title: Trailing off — ending a sentence to imply "...and more unsaid"
content:
# Trailing off — ending a sentence to imply "...and more unsaid"

A genuinely common Japanese conversational habit: ending a sentence right at a connector (けど, し, から, て-form) without ever finishing the thought. The connector itself signals "there's more to this, but I'll let you fill in the rest" — it's not a grammatical mistake or an interrupted sentence, it's a deliberate softening/politeness technique. Ties together threads already mentioned individually in [[../1-particle/12-けど]], [[../1-particle/15-し]], and [[../5-filler/5-ちょっと]].

## Why trail off at all
Finishing a sentence completely — stating a full request, a full refusal, a full opinion — can land as more forceful or final than intended. Stopping right at the connector leaves the conclusion implicit, which reads as softer, more polite, and less confrontational. The listener understands exactly what's being implied; it just isn't said outright.

## けど — trailing before a request or opinion
Covered in [[../1-particle/12-けど]], but worth seeing as part of the bigger pattern: けど at the end of a sentence sets up an unstated "...so [can you help / what do you think / etc.]":

- すみません、ちょっと聞きたいんですけど。— Excuse me, [I] wanted to ask something... (implies: "...so, can I?")
- これ、いいと思うんですけど。— I think this is good, but... (implies: "...what do you think?" or "...so let's go with it, unless you object")

## し — trailing as a loose, shrugging justification
Covered in [[../1-particle/15-し]]: a sentence ending on し implies "...and there's more reasons like this," without listing them all — reads as a casual, semi-complete justification:

- でも、疲れてるし。— But, [I]'m tired, [you know]. (implies: "...so let's not / so give me a break," left unstated)

## から — trailing before an implied conclusion
から (see [[../1-particle/8a-から]]) can trail the same way, leaving the "so..." conclusion unstated when it's obvious from context:

- もう遅いから...。— It's already late, so... (implied: "...we should go / you should leave / let's wrap up")

## て-form — trailing as a soft, unfinished request
A bare て-form (see [[../2-verb/2-て-form]]) at the end of an utterance can similarly leave a fuller request implicit, especially in pleading or emotional contexts:

- お願い、聞いて...。— Please, listen [to me]... (trails into an unstated "...just this once" or similar)

## ちょっと — trailing as a soft refusal
A different flavor of the same mechanic, covered in [[../5-filler/5-ちょっと]]: trailing off right after ちょっと is the standard, expected way to decline something without a blunt "no":

- 今日はちょっと...。— Today's a bit... (declining, fully understood without finishing)

## The common thread
In every case, the sentence is *structurally* incomplete but *pragmatically* complete — the listener isn't left confused, they're being given room to not force a direct confrontation, refusal, or demand into the open. This is one of the more distinctly Japanese conversational habits, and recognizing it (rather than waiting for someone to "finish their sentence") is important for following natural daily speech.

## Notes
- Rising, soft intonation on the trailing connector signals this is intentional, not a false start or a memory lapse — tone carries a lot of the meaning here, same as with ね (see [[../1-particle/6a-ね]]).
- As a learner, you don't need to master producing this yourself early on — recognizing it in others' speech (and not waiting awkwardly for them to "finish") is the higher-value skill to build first.

title: から - "from" / "because" particle
content:
# から - "from" / "because" particle

Two distinct jobs: marking a starting point (time/place), and marking a reason/cause. They look identical but attach to different things — see [[8b-まで]] for the "until" counterpart that pairs with から's starting-point use.

## Starting point: time/place "from"
Marks where or when something begins:

- 9時から始まります。— [It] starts from 9 o'clock.
- 家から駅まで歩きます。— [I] walk from home to the station. (see [[8b-まで]] for the から〜まで pair)
- 大阪から来ました。— [I] came from Osaka.

## Source / origin (broader than physical start)
から also marks where something originates from more abstractly — who gave/told/made something, or what something is derived from:

- 先生から聞きました。— [I] heard [it] from the teacher.
- 友達から手紙が来た。— A letter came from a friend.
- 米から作られる。— [It]'s made from rice.

Compare with に as indirect object (see [[3a-に]]): 先生に聞きました (I asked the teacher — targeting them) vs 先生から聞きました (I heard it from the teacher — them as the source). Different verbs, different direction of information flow.

## Reason/cause: "because"
Attaches to the end of a clause (after plain or polite form) to give a reason — the から-clause comes first, the result/conclusion follows:

- 疲れたから、休みます。— Because [I]'m tired, [I]'ll rest.
- 雨が降っているから、行きたくない。— Since it's raining, [I] don't want to go.
- 危ないから、気をつけて。— [It]'s dangerous, so be careful.

Unlike the particle use (which attaches only to nouns), reason-から attaches to a full clause — verb, adjective, or noun+だ/です:

- 学生だから、お金がない。— Since [I]'m a student, [I] don't have money. (plain だ before から, even in a polite conversation — see [[3-plain-vs-polite-form]])
- 忙しいですから、行けません。— [I]'m busy, so [I] can't go. (polite です before から is also fine — unlike と思う, から doesn't force plain form)

## から vs ので (reason particles — brief note)
から is more direct/assertive about the cause; ので is softer and more common in polite/formal explanations. から is the safer daily default — ので is a later refinement, not needed to start.

## Notes
- から can stack after は for contrast: 明日からは頑張ります。— Starting tomorrow, [I]'ll work hard [implying: unlike until now].
- てから is a related but distinct pattern: て-form + から means "after doing X" (sequencing, not reason) — 食べてから、寝ます。— [I]'ll sleep after eating. Don't confuse this with plain-form+から (reason).

title: まで - "until/up to" particle
content:
# まで - "until/up to" particle

Marks an endpoint — in time, space, or extent. Pairs naturally with [[8a-から]] to bracket a range: から marks where something starts, まで marks where it ends.

## Endpoint: time/place "until/to"
- 9時まで働きます。— [I] work until 9 o'clock.
- 駅まで歩きます。— [I] walk to/as far as the station.
- 家から駅まで10分です。— [It]'s 10 minutes from home to the station.

The から〜まで pairing is the standard way to express a range with a clear start and end:

- 月曜日から金曜日まで働きます。— [I] work from Monday to Friday.
- 東京から大阪まで新幹線で行きました。— [I] went from Tokyo to Osaka by shinkansen.

## まで alone (no から needed)
まで works fine without a stated starting point — the start is just whatever "now"/the default reference point is:

- 明日まで待ってください。— Please wait until tomorrow.
- ここまでできました。— [I]'ve gotten this far. / [I]'ve done up to here.

## まで vs までに — a critical distinction
This is the single most important thing to get right with まで: **まで** means the action/state continues *up through* the endpoint, while **までに** means the action must happen *by* (at some point no later than) the deadline — a one-time event, not a continuous state:

- 5時まで待ちます。— [I]'ll wait until 5. (waiting continues the whole time, up to 5)
- 5時までに来てください。— Please come by 5. (arrival happens at some point no later than 5 — not "arriving continuously")

Mixing these up is a common, meaning-changing mistake:
- 明日まで終わらせます。would oddly suggest "finishing" as an ongoing state through tomorrow.
- 明日までに終わらせます。— [I]'ll get [it] finished by tomorrow. (correct — finishing is a one-time event with a deadline)

Rule of thumb: if the verb describes something continuous/ongoing (待つ, 働く, いる), use plain まで. If the verb describes a one-time completed event (終わる, 出す, 来る, 提出する), use までに.

## Extent: "even/as far as" (emphatic)
Like も (see [[5b-も]]), まで can push toward an extreme, emphatic reading — "even," "to the extent of":

- 彼は私にまで嘘をついた。— He lied even to me.
- そこまで言わなくても。— [You] didn't have to go that far [in what you said]. (lit. "even to that point")

## Notes
- まで doesn't replace は/が/を the way many other particles do — it can combine with は for contrast: 5時までは大丈夫です。— Until 5, [it]'s fine [implying: after that, it's not].
- Don't confuse まで (until, this file) with 〜前に (before) — 5時まで (up until 5, inclusive of the whole span) vs 5時前に (before 5, i.e. sometime earlier than 5) describe different things.

title: だけ - "only" (neutral) particle
content:
# だけ - "only" (neutral) particle

Marks a strict limit — "only X," "just X" — in either affirmative or negative sentences, with a neutral, matter-of-fact tone. See [[9b-しか]] for the negative-only counterpart with a different nuance.

## Basic "only"
Attaches directly to nouns, replacing は/が/を much like も does (see [[5b-も]]):

- 千円だけあります。— [I] only have 1000 yen. (stated as plain fact)
- これだけください。— Please give [me] just this.
- 少しだけ食べました。— [I] ate just a little.

## Works in affirmative sentences (unlike しか)
だけ is fine standing alone with a positive verb — this is the key structural difference from しか, which forces a negative verb:

- 水だけ飲みます。— [I]'ll only drink water. (plain affirmative, no negative needed)

## だけ with verbs/clauses
だけ can attach after a plain-form verb or clause, not just nouns, meaning "only [do X]" or "just because [X]":

- 見るだけです。— [I]'m just looking. (common in shops, deflecting a salesperson)
- 言っただけです。— [I] just said [it, no deeper meaning].

## Tone: neutral, not emotional
だけ simply states a limit without extra feeling — compare with しか, which carries a stronger "that's all there is, and it feels insufficient" undertone (see [[9b-しか]]). だけ is the safer, more neutral default when you just want to say "only."

## Notes
- だけ can combine with で: 一人だけで行った。— [I] went alone, just by myself.
- だけじゃなく(て) — "not only" — sets up a "not only X, but also Y" pattern: 日本語だけじゃなく、中国語も話せます。— [I] can speak not only Japanese, but also Chinese [see [[5b-も]] for the も half of this pattern].

title: しか - "only" (negative-forced) particle
content:
# しか - "only" (negative-forced) particle

Also means "only," but structurally different from [[9a-だけ]] in one strict way: しか always requires a negative verb at the end of the sentence, and carries a stronger "that's all there is" undertone — often implying it's less than [you] wanted/expected.

## Must pair with a negative verb
This is the one hard rule to remember — しか + affirmative verb is ungrammatical:

- 千円しかありません。— [I] only have 1000 yen. (lit. "there isn't [anything] except 1000 yen")
- ~~千円しかあります。~~ — ungrammatical, must be negative.
- 日本語しか話せません。— [I] can only speak Japanese [and no other language].
- 少ししか食べなかった。— [I] only ate a little. (implying: less than expected/hoped)

The double-negative logic ("nothing except X") is baked into the grammar even though the English translation reads as a plain positive statement ("I only have...").

## しか vs だけ — the nuance difference
Both can translate to "only," but they don't feel the same:

| | だけ | しか |
|---|---|---|
| Verb form | either | must be negative |
| Tone | neutral | implies insufficiency/regret |
| Example | 水だけ飲みます。(I'll just drink water — neutral choice) | 水しかありません。(There's only water — implying "that's all there is, sorry") |

If you want to express mild disappointment or emphasize scarcity, reach for しか. If you're just stating a plain limit, だけ is safer and more neutral.

## Common daily patterns
- 〜人しかいない — "there are only [N] people" (often implying too few): 三人しかいません。— There are only 3 people [and that's not enough].
- 〜しかない — "there's no choice but to..." (idiomatic, beyond literal "only"): やるしかない。— [There's] nothing to do but try. / [I] have no choice but to do it.

## Notes
- しか replaces は/が/を on the noun it attaches to, same as だけ and も.
- しか can stack after other particles: これしか道がない。— This is the only path [there is].

title: ぐらい / くらい - "about/approximately" particle
content:
# ぐらい / くらい - "about/approximately" particle

Marks a rough estimate — amount, time, degree — rather than an exact figure. Both spellings/pronunciations are used interchangeably (くらい is slightly more common in careful/formal speech, ぐらい in casual speech), no meaning difference.

## Approximate quantity
Attaches after a number/amount to soften it into an estimate:

- 3時間ぐらい待ちました。— [I] waited about 3 hours.
- 千円くらいです。— [It]'s about 1000 yen.
- 10人ぐらい来ました。— About 10 people came.

## Approximate degree (comparison of scale)
ぐらい/くらい can also express "to the extent of," comparing a degree or intensity rather than a quantity — often paired with a noun/clause as the reference point:

- 死ぬぐらい疲れた。— [I]'m tired to the point of [almost] dying. (hyperbolic, very common casual exaggeration)
- 彼ぐらい上手じゃない。— [I]'m not as skilled as him. (roughly "to his degree")

## それぐらい / どのぐらい — common set phrases
- それぐらい分かるよ。— [I] know [at least] that much. (mild pushback, "give me some credit")
- どのぐらいかかりますか。— About how long does [it] take? (asking for an estimate — extremely common daily question, alongside どれぐらい)

## ぐらい vs ほど — brief note
ほど is a more formal/written near-synonym for the "degree/extent" sense of ぐらい — 〜ほど not needed as a first pass; ぐらい/くらい covers casual daily use fine on its own.

## Notes
- ぐらい/くらいはdoesn't replace は/が/を the way だけ/しか/も do — it attaches to the quantity/degree expression itself, which then behaves normally in the sentence (3時間ぐらい待った — ぐらい sits between the quantity and the verb, no particle conflict).
- Can combine with other particles: 3時間ぐらいで着きます。— [We]'ll arrive in about 3 hours. (ぐらい + で, marking the approximate duration as a bounding scope — see [[3b-で]]).

title: ながら - "while doing" particle
content:
# ながら - "while doing" particle

Links two actions happening at the same time, done by the same person — "while doing X, [also do] Y." Attaches to the ます-stem (see [[1-conjugation-group]] in 2-verb), not the dictionary form.

## Forming it
ます-stem + ながら:

- 食べる → 食べながら — while eating
- 話す → 話しながら — while talking
- 歩く → 歩きながら — while walking
- する → しながら — while doing

## Core pattern
**A-ながら、B** → "while doing A, [do] B" — B is the main action, A is the background/simultaneous one:

- 音楽を聞きながら勉強します。— [I] study while listening to music.
- 歩きながらスマホを見るのは危ない。— Looking at your phone while walking is dangerous.
- テレビを見ながらご飯を食べた。— [I] ate while watching TV.

The subject must be the same person doing both actions — ながら can't link two different people's simultaneous actions.

## Word order matters for emphasis
The verb after ながら (B) is the main, foregrounded action; the ながら-clause (A) is the backdrop. Swapping which action goes where changes what's emphasized:

- 音楽を聞きながら勉強する。— [I] study (main) while listening to music (background).
- 勉強しながら音楽を聞く。— [I] listen to music (main) while studying (background).

Same two activities, different emphasis depending on which one is the "point" of the sentence.

## ながら as "despite/although" (secondary use)
A less common but real second meaning: ながら can mean "even though," especially in the fixed phrase 残念ながら:

- 残念ながら、行けません。— Unfortunately (lit. "while it's regrettable"), [I] can't go.
- 知っていながら、教えてくれなかった。— Even though [he] knew, [he] didn't tell [me].

This use is lower-frequency than the simultaneous-action use but 残念ながら itself is common enough as a fixed phrase to recognize on sight.

## Notes
- Don't confuse ながら (same person, two simultaneous actions) with て-form sequencing (see [[2-て-form]] in 2-verb), which describes actions happening one after another, not at the same time.
- Casual daily speech uses this constantly for everyday multitasking descriptions — one of the more naturally-produced patterns once the ます-stem is solid.

title: けど - casual "but" particle
content:
# けど - casual "but" particle

Casual version of が (as a clause-connector, not the subject particle covered in [[1b-が]]) and でも — links two clauses in contrast, or just softens a statement. Extremely common in daily speech.

## Basic contrast: "but"
Attaches after plain or polite form, connecting two clauses where the second contradicts or contrasts with the first:

- 行きたいけど、時間がない。— [I] want to go, but [I] don't have time.
- 高いけど、おいしいです。— [It]'s expensive, but [it]'s good.
- 忙しいですけど、大丈夫です。— [I]'m busy, but [it]'s fine. (polite form + けど is fine — けど doesn't force plain form, like から)

Formality ladder: けど (most casual) → けれど → けれども (most formal/written). All three mean the same thing; けど is what you'll hear constantly in daily conversation.

## Softening / cushioning (no real contrast)
Just like the softening use of が in formal speech, けど often appears with nothing actually being contrasted — it just takes the edge off a statement, request, or opinion:

- これ、いいと思うんですけど。— I think this is good, [but/well...]. (hedging an opinion, inviting reaction)
- すみません、ちょっと聞きたいんですけど。— Excuse me, [I] wanted to ask something... (softening a request before making it)

This trailing-off use — ending a sentence right at けど without finishing the thought — is one of the most natural-sounding casual speech habits once you notice it. It leaves room for the listener to respond rather than steamrolling with a complete statement. See [[../8-conjunction/2-trailing-off]] for this pattern across けど/し/から/て-form as a unified habit.

## けど introducing background before the main point
けど is also used to set up context before getting to what you actually want to say, similar to English "so, [background]... anyway, [point]":

- 昨日話したことなんだけど、やっぱり無理かも。— About what [we] talked about yesterday... [I] think it might not work after all.

## Notes
- けど doesn't replace は/が/を — it attaches to the end of a complete clause, not to a noun.
- Don't confuse this けど with けど as a shortened, casual sentence-final softener with no contrast at all — context (is there an actual contrast, or is it just trailing off) tells you which reading applies, both are common.

title: とか - casual "or something/like" particle
content:
# とか - casual "or something/like" particle

Casual, hedging version of と (see [[5a-と]]) for listing examples — signals "this and stuff like it," not an exhaustive list. Extremely common in relaxed daily speech.

## Non-exhaustive listing ("...and stuff", "...or whatever")
Where と lists items completely (see [[5a-と]]), とか implies there are other similar things left unsaid — softer, more casual, "for example":

- パンとかコーヒーとか買いました。— [I] bought bread, coffee, and stuff like that.
- 週末は映画とか見ます。— On weekends [I] watch movies and stuff.

Often only appears once, at the end of a single example, functioning like "or something":

- 疲れたから、休むとか。— [I]'m tired, so maybe [I'll] rest or something. (very casual, trailing suggestion)

## Softening an example or suggestion
とか frequently marks something as just one option among many, keeping the tone light and non-committal — useful for suggestions without sounding pushy:

- お茶とか、どう? — How about tea or something?
- 明日とか、暇? — Are [you] free tomorrow or [some other day nearby]?

## Quoting/hedged reporting (casual version of と + 言う)
とか can casually report what someone said, with a slightly detached, "or something like that" flavor — less precise/committal than と言っていた:

- 田中さん、来ないとか言ってたよ。— Tanaka said something about not coming, [I think].

This carries a "secondhand, not 100% sure of the exact wording" nuance that plain と + 言う doesn't have.

## とか vs や — both non-exhaustive, different register
や (not yet covered as its own file) is the more neutral/written non-exhaustive "and" (パンやコーヒーを買いました。); とか is its casual-speech cousin with the added "or something" hedge. In daily conversation, とか is far more common than や.

## Notes
- とか doesn't replace は/が/を — it attaches directly after the nouns/clauses being listed, and the whole とか-list can still take a particle afterward (パンとかコーヒーとかを買いました. — the final を marks the whole list as the object, though it's often dropped in casual speech per [[2-を]]).
- Overusing とか as a verbal tic (like English "like" or "or whatever") is common in very casual youth speech — recognize it, but don't feel pressured to overuse it yourself.

title: し - casual "and, what's more" (reason-stacking) particle
content:
# し - casual "and, what's more" (reason-stacking) particle

Lists reasons or facts, implying there are more where that came from — "X, and also Y, [so...]." Distinct from から (see [[8a-から]]), which gives a single, direct reason; し stacks multiple points loosely, often for a casual explanation or complaint.

## Forming it
Attaches after plain form (verbs, い-adjectives, and な-adjectives/nouns + だ):

- 忙しいし、疲れてるし、今日は休む。— [I]'m busy, and [I]'m tired, so [I]'m resting today.
- このレストラン、安いし、おいしいし、また来たい。— This restaurant is cheap, and tasty, so [I] want to come again.
- 今日は雨だし、寒いし、出かけたくない。— Today it's rainy, and it's cold, so [I] don't want to go out.

## One し is enough — doesn't need to be doubled
Unlike も...も (see [[5b-も]]) or the examples above, a single し at the end of one clause already implies "and there's more" even without a second し stacking another clause:

- 疲れたし、もう寝る。— [I]'m tired, so [I]'m going to sleep. (one reason stated, but し signals "among other things")

## し vs から/ので — tone difference
から/ので present a direct, singular cause → effect. し presents a looser list of contributing factors, often used to justify a decision without sounding like [you]'re over-explaining or being defensive — a very natural way to casually rationalize something:

- 疲れたから、休む。— Because [I]'m tired, [I]'ll rest. (direct, single reason)
- 疲れたし、休む。— [I]'m tired, [and stuff], so [I]'ll rest. (looser, casual, implies unstated additional reasons)

## Standalone use — trailing justification
し can end a sentence on its own as a shrugging, semi-complete justification, similar to how English "...and stuff" or "I mean..." trails off:

- でも、疲れてるし。— But, [I]'m tired, [you know]. (trailing off, offering a loose excuse)

See [[../8-conjunction/2-trailing-off]] for this same habit across けど/し/から/て-form.

## Notes
- し doesn't replace は/が/を — it attaches to the end of a complete clause, like けど (see [[12-けど]]).
- Casual, everyday register — safe in relaxed conversation, less common in formal/written contexts where から/ので or a fuller list would be preferred.

title: ばかり - "just did X" / "only, all X" particle
content:
# ばかり - "just did X" / "only, all X" particle

Two related but distinct uses: marking something as having *just* happened, or marking something as happening *excessively/exclusively*. Different nuance from だけ/しか (see [[9a-だけ]]/[[9b-しか]]), which are about strict limits, not recency or repetition.

## Just did X — たばかり
Attaches after plain past (た-form, see [[../2-verb/2-て-form]] for the sound-shift table) to mean "just did," emphasizing how recently something happened:

- 食べたばかりです。— [I] just ate.
- 日本に来たばかりです。— [I] just came to Japan [recently].
- 始めたばかりで、まだよく分かりません。— [I] just started, so [I] don't really understand [it] yet.

This is a distinct, common daily pattern — different from さっき (a moment ago, a plain adverb) in that ばかり grammatically frames the *state of having just done it* as still relevant/fresh.

## Only/all X — excessive repetition or exclusivity
Attaches after nouns (with を often dropped) or plain form, meaning "nothing but X," "always doing X" — usually with a mildly critical or exasperated tone:

- 彼はゲームばかりしている。— He's always playing games [and nothing else]. (see [[../2-verb/9-ている]] for the ている state)
- お菓子ばかり食べないで。— Don't eat nothing but sweets. (see [[../4-pattern/2-requests]] for ないで as a casual negative request)
- 文句ばかり言う。— [He] does nothing but complain.

This use carries an implicit "...and that's a problem" undertone — different from だけ, which is neutral about the limit it states.

## ばかり vs たばかり — don't confuse the two
Same word, different attachment point, different meaning entirely:

| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 動詞た形 + ばかり | just did X (recency) |
| 名詞/動詞 + ばかり | only/always X (excess, mild criticism) |

## Notes
- ばかり can combine with いる for a compound state: 泣いてばかりいる。— [She]'s always crying. (て-form + ばかり + いる)
- Casual speech often shortens ばかり to just ばっかり or ばっか — same meaning, more emphatic/colloquial: ゲームばっかり! — Nothing but games!

title: Verb conjugation groups
content:
# Verb conjugation groups

Japanese verbs split into three groups by how they conjugate. Everything downstream — て-form, plain form, potential, negative, conditional — is a mechanical rule applied on top of this grouping. Learn to classify a verb correctly first; the rest is pattern application. See [[2-て-form]] and [[3-plain-vs-polite-form]], both built directly on this.

## The three groups

**Group 1 — う-verbs (godan / "u-verbs")**
Dictionary form ends in -u, and the final kana is any u-row kana other than る preceded by an i/e sound (see the る-verb trap below):

- 話す (hanasu) — to speak
- 読む (yomu) — to read
- 買う (kau) — to buy
- 待つ (matsu) — to wait
- 帰る (kaeru) — to return (looks like a る-verb, isn't — see below)

**Group 2 — る-verbs (ichidan / "ru-verbs")**
Dictionary form ends in -iru or -eru, where removing る leaves a valid stem directly usable across all conjugations:

- 食べる (taberu) — to eat
- 見る (miru) — to see
- 起きる (okiru) — to get up
- 寝る (neru) — to sleep

**Group 3 — irregular**
Only two true irregulars, but they're extremely high-frequency:

- する — to do
- 来る (kuru) — to come

## The る-verb trap
Not every verb ending in -iru/-eru is a る-verb. Some are secretly う-verbs that happen to end in る:

- 帰る (kaeru) — to return → う-verb (conjugates 帰ります, not 帰えます)
- 入る (hairu) — to enter → う-verb
- 走る (hashiru) — to run → う-verb
- 知る (shiru) — to know → う-verb

There's no 100% reliable shortcut — these have to be memorized as exceptions. When in doubt, check the ます-form: real る-verbs drop る cleanly (食べる→食べます), fake ones (う-verbs in disguise) change the vowel (帰る→帰ります, not 帰ます).

## ます-stem (masu-stem)
The single most useful form to extract from any verb — nearly every conjugation pattern builds off it:

| Group | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| う-verb | change final -u to -i | 話す → 話し |
| る-verb | drop る | 食べる → 食べ |
| irregular | する→し, 来る→来(き) | する → し, 来る → 来 |

Add ます for polite non-past: 話します, 食べます, します, 来ます (きます).

## Why this matters before anything else
て-form, た-form (plain past), potential form, passive, causative — all of them are group-dependent rules. If you can't reliably say "this is a う-verb" vs "this is a る-verb," every subsequent pattern becomes rote memorization per-verb instead of a rule applied once. Nail this first.

## Notes
- 一段 (ichidan) = "one grade" = る-verb (stem doesn't change). 五段 (godan) = "five grades" = う-verb (stem shifts across the five u-row vowels: か/き/く/け/こ etc.) — the Japanese grammar terms literally describe the mechanic.
- Dictionary form is also called plain non-past — see [[3-plain-vs-polite-form]].

title: て-form
content:
# て-form

The single highest-leverage conjugation in Japanese — see [[0-overview]] point 2. Once you can produce it reliably, most of daily grammar is just attaching things to it. Built directly from the conjugation groups in [[1-conjugation-group]] — make sure that's solid first.

## Forming て-form by group

**る-verbs (Group 2) — trivial**
Drop る, add て:

- 食べる → 食べて
- 見る → 見て
- 起きる → 起きて

**Irregulars (Group 3)**
- する → して
- 来る (kuru) → 来て (きて)

**う-verbs (Group 1) — the sound-shift rules**
The ending determines the shift. These are worth drilling until automatic:

| Ending | Rule | Example |
|---|---|---|
| う, つ, る | → って | 買う→買って, 待つ→待って, 帰る→帰って |
| む, ぶ, ぬ | → んで | 読む→読んで, 遊ぶ→遊んで, 死ぬ→死んで |
| く | → いて | 書く→書いて |
| ぐ | → いで | 泳ぐ→泳いで |
| す | → して | 話す→話して |

Exception: 行く (iku, "to go") is irregular within this pattern — 行って, not 行いて.

Same shifts apply to plain past (た-form): って/んで/いて/いで/して → just swap the final て for た (行って→行った). Learning て-form well means た-form comes almost for free.

## What attaches to て-form
This is the part that makes て-form the "hub" — a small set of endings turn it into most of daily grammar:

- 食べて + ください → please eat
- 食べて + いる → eating / (state of having eaten, context-dependent)
- 食べて + もいい → allowed to eat
- 食べて + はいけない → not allowed to eat
- 食べて + みる → try eating
- 食べて + おく → eat in preparation / ahead of time
- 食べて + しまう → end up eating / eat completely (often regret/completion nuance)
- 食べて、飲んで、寝た → sequencing actions ("ate, drank, [then] slept")

## てくる / ていく — change over time
Two more て-form attachments, specifically for describing something unfolding across time rather than a fixed state. Both come from くる (to come) and いく (to go), but used abstractly rather than about physical movement:

**てくる — a change that's been happening up to now, moving toward the present**
- 天気が良くなってきた。— The weather's been getting better [and continues to now].
- 日本語が分かるようになってきた。— [I]'ve gradually come to understand Japanese.
- 雨が降ってきた。— It's started raining. (a change beginning, arriving at the present moment)

**ていく — a change that will continue on from now, moving toward the future**
- これからも頑張っていきます。— [I]'ll keep doing my best going forward.
- 少しずつ人口が減っていく。— The population will keep gradually decreasing [from here on].
- 子供はどんどん大きくなっていく。— Kids just keep growing bigger and bigger [as time goes on].

The core intuition: てくる pulls a trend up to *now* (often from the past), ていく pushes a trend forward from *now* (into the future). Both are common in daily narration about gradual change — weather, feelings, habits, life circumstances — not just literal coming/going.

## て-form for sequencing vs. simultaneous connecting
When chaining clauses with て, the actions are read as sequential (and often causally/temporally linked), not just "and":

- 顔を洗って、歯を磨いた。— [I] washed my face, [then] brushed my teeth.
- 熱があって、休みました。— [I] had a fever, so [I] rested. (て can carry a loose cause-effect reading)

## Notes
- て-form itself carries no tense — tense comes from whatever attaches after it, or from context if it ends a casual sentence (食べて! as a soft command).
- Get the う-verb sound-shift table (って/んで/いて/いで/して) to muscle memory before moving on — it's the one part of Japanese conjugation most worth over-drilling.

title: Plain vs. polite (です/ます) form
content:
# Plain vs. polite (です/ます) form

Japanese runs on two parallel registers for nearly every verb and adjective. This isn't optional politeness dressing — see [[0-overview]] point 3 — it's a structural axis: certain grammar patterns require plain form even inside an otherwise polite sentence.

## The two registers

**Polite (です/ます)** — used with strangers, coworkers, service interactions, formal writing, and by default when unsure:

- 食べます / 食べません / 食べました / 食べませんでした
- 学生です / 学生ではありません (or じゃないです, more casual-polite)

**Plain (辞書形)** — used with friends, family, inner thought, casual writing, and *inside* longer sentences regardless of the overall politeness level:

- 食べる / 食べない / 食べた / 食べなかった
- 学生だ / 学生じゃない

## Conjugation table (verbs)

| | Polite | Plain |
|---|---|---|
| Non-past affirmative | 食べます | 食べる |
| Non-past negative | 食べません | 食べない |
| Past affirmative | 食べました | 食べた |
| Past negative | 食べませんでした | 食べなかった |

う-verb plain negative: drop -u, add -anai (行く→行かない, 話す→話さない — う irregularly becomes わ: 買う→買わない). Plain past follows the same sound-shift as て-form (see [[2-て-form]]): 行って→行った.

## Copula (だ/です) table

| | Polite | Plain |
|---|---|---|
| Affirmative | 学生です | 学生だ |
| Negative | 学生じゃないです | 学生じゃない |
| Past affirmative | 学生でした | 学生だった |
| Past negative | 学生じゃなかったです | 学生じゃなかった |

だ is often dropped entirely in casual speech when it's the final word of a plain sentence (学生。just standing alone) — but it reappears before だろう, だと思う, etc.

## Why plain form is required mid-sentence
A long list of grammar patterns attach to plain form regardless of the sentence's overall politeness — this is the "structural axis" point:

- 〜と思う: 雨が降ると思います。— I think it'll rain. (降る is plain, even though the sentence ends politely with 思います)
- 〜んです: 疲れたんです。— [explaining:] I'm tired. (plain 疲れた + んです, not 疲れましたんです)
- Before ようだ, らしい, し, けど (casual), and inside relative clauses modifying nouns: 昨日買った本 — the book [I] bought yesterday (買った is plain even in an otherwise polite conversation)

Mixing this up — trying ます before と思う, for instance — is one of the most common beginner errors once sentences get longer than a single clause.

## When to use which
- Default to polite (です/ます) in speech with anyone you're not close to, and in first encounters — it's the safe default.
- Plain form is not "ruder," it's a different social register — used with close friends/family, in diaries/casual writing, in your own internal monologue (と思う clauses), and it's also what dictionaries, grammar explanations, and most example sentences default to as the "base" form.
- Within one conversation, don't randomly alternate です/ます and plain endings on main clauses — pick a register and stay consistent; only the mid-sentence plain-form rule above is an exception.

## Notes
- Plain non-past = dictionary form — the same form used for classifying conjugation groups in [[1-conjugation-group]].
- な-adjectives and the copula behave alike (だ/です pattern); い-adjectives conjugate on their own without needing だ/です for plain form (see the upcoming adjective notes) — い-adjective plain non-past is just the adjective itself: 高い, not 高いだ.
